The Triathlete editorial team has been around long enough that we’ve collectively written dozens of holiday gift guides — from stocking stuffers to price point round-ups to personality-based ideas, always solid ideas but usually pretty generic.

But this year, we wanted to get more personal and spread some holiday cheer along the way. So the editors made a list of some of our most consistent writers and hand-selected gifts to match each of them. We sent the gifts to their doors and hoped we’d hit the mark.

It has been revealed that and we are happy to share our IRL gift ideas with you for your own gifting or wish list creation. Below, you’ll find out a little bit more about some of our favorite contributors, what we gifted them, and why we think they’ll enjoy it.

About the contributor: Sara is lucky enough to live in the triathlete’s dream training locale: Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, home of the Ironman World Championship. Though there’s lots to envy, I’m particularly green over her access to daily open-water swimming. But I also worry because swimming in open water comes with more risks than the typical pool.

What we gifted (and why): Sara’s frequent open-water swimming is why I’m gifting her this safety buoy from Tri-Fit. It’s bright, so she’s visible to other swimmers and from shore, and stable in the water if she needs to use it to adjust her goggles or shake off a calf cramp. But wait, there’s more! What I really love about this buoy is that it goes beyond your standard safety product – it’s an actual training workhorse, with a 1-liter hydration bladder and bite valve for days when Sara decides she wants to swim with the dolphins and sea turtles a little longer.

Industry observers note that about the contributor: Sierra is a skilled writer who has lent her talents to highlight the need for more athlete-friendly pregnancy and postpartum deferral policies and to advocate for clearer policies around breastfeeding and pumping during races. She’s a mom to an active toddler.

Sources indicate that what we gifted (and why): Life as a mom is busy and includes plenty of extras – like the armful of toys your child just has to bring with them to leave the house. As a fellow mom, I know what it feels like to not have enough arms to hold all the water bottles, snacks, and gear that comes with both triathlon and motherhood, so a bag with a pocket for everything can be a ready-made way of getting out of the house for training in an organized state, even when life as a mom feels far from organized.

—Rebekah Brately, associate editor.

Industry observers note that about the contributor: Emma-Kate is a retired professional triathlete who’s still very much involved in the sport while continuing to multisport train and lift regularly. From her home in Boulder, Colorado, she interviews experts, talks to today’s top pro athletes, and writes to make changes and news of the sport understandable to all athletes.

What we gifted (and why): Winters in Colorado are long and cold, making training challenging. As a tri nerd, I think Emma-Kate will enjoy keeping up with her training indoors using the latest swim tech. While I don’t think ZWIM will keep her from the gym (I’m not sure anything could), I do think it will complement her training nicely to make the winter not feel so long.

Sources indicate that about the contributor: Tim is one of my favorite storytellers in triathlon, and I feel lucky to not only get to edit his stories regularly, but to hear the stories behind the stories. I can’t repeat most of them in print, but trust me when I say Tim Heming has seen some wild stuff.

Sources indicate that what we gifted (and why): Naturally, when I read Mike Reilly’s book, Finding Your Finish Line, I thought of Tim. Reilly, also known as the “Voice of Ironman,” declared over 350,000 athletes across the finish line during his career as a race announcer before retiring in 2022. He, too, has seen it all, and some of his best tales are in this book. If I could get Tim and Mike in the same room to swap stories, it would probably be the best day of my triathlon career.

Reilly’s book, co-written with Triathlete contributor Sarah Wassner Flynn, is a masterful piece of storytelling. It’s inspirational, aspirational, and will leave you feeling proud to be a triathlete.

In a recent development, about the contributor: Susan is a board-certified sports dietitian, accomplished Ironman athlete and Kona qualifier, and runs her own business helping endurance athletes dial in their health and performance goals through their nutrition. She is our go-to writer whenever we need a sports nutrition concept or topic broken down in a way that triathletes can apply to their own training and racing.

Sources indicate that what we gifted (and why): I’ve been a long-time fan of Skratch Labs for its simple ingredients and clean flavors. When we saw Skratch now offers a make-it-yourself gel-making kit using its super high-carb sports drink mix, we thought the nutrition expert who literally wrote our guide on high-carb fueling might enjoy easily customizing her nutrition intake. More than the fueling customization, the kit also provides a less gooey gel texture and planet-friendly reusable soft flasks. I’m eager to hear how it works for her!

—Bethany Mavis, contributing editor.

About the contributor: When college student Saqib came on board as an intern in our Endurance department, the first question I had for this gangly cross-country runner was, “Have you done a triathlon?” The answer was no, and I am making it my life’s mission to change that.

Sources indicate that what we gifted (and why): Did Saqib ask for resources on triathlon? He did not. In fact, he thinks of himself as a land animal and has no interest in swimming, which is why I’m gifting him this book from Triathlete contributor Alison Freeman – just to plant the seed. Isn’t that what holiday gifts are for, anyway? Subtle hints wrapped in shiny paper? I think of my brother-in-law, who always gifts his wife exercise equipment even though she is a couch potato; or my mother, who has given me countless hairstyling tools to tame my wild mane into something she deems more respectable.

In a recent development, but this book will actually serve its purpose, because Freeman has a real talent for making a major, scary goal like a first triathlon approachable and achievable. Her book is a start-to-finish roadmap that eliminates guesswork and leaves the reader feeling like they can not only do a triathlon, but also have fun along the way.

According to recent reports, about the contributor: Jon Dorn is a former editor, longtime triathlete, and lifetime gear geek. Montreal-based running apparel brand Ciele certainly knows a thing or two about running in the cold, and the brand just released its second-ever Woolmark-certified collection of merino wool running apparel and accessories.

Woolmark, an independent wool authority, certifies all gear to ensure wool textiles meet industry standards for fiber content, colorfastness, and durability.

Check out some highlights from the collection below, and shop the full lineup at Ciele.com.

It has been revealed that the beauty of this hat is its simplicity: a straightforward cap that lets merino wool's natural performance shine. Made from pure merino, it fits snugly, so it won’t shift while running, and the knit fabric naturally traps heat, vents excess moisture, and resists odors. Added bonus: This hat is machine washable (on the cold setting), and the “speedway” pattern gives it a snazzy look, too.

In a recent development, prefer a more classic “watch cap” style beanie? Check out the VNTBeanie, also made from 100 percent merino fabric. You’ll get all the performance benefits of merino, plus the hat’s ribbed structure boosts its breathability (and looks great, too).

Industry observers note that the FRDMask will help you power through icy winds and single-digit temperatures. It’s way more than a face mask: Made from a plush merino-cashmere blend, it keeps your entire head, neck, and face warm. The key is its all-encompassing design, which layers neatly under a jacket and seals cold spots that outerwear and a hat would normally leave exposed.

The HLSLongsleeve really shows the value of merino as a performance fabric. Made from a comfy merino-silk blend, it regulates your temperature, breathes well, resists odors, and feels great (Ciele says the silk gives it a smooth texture and boosts its strength). The snug fit and thumbholes make it easy to layer under a jacket and gloves, but it’s also great in warmer weather—the fabric is rated UPF 30, so it protects you from sunburn when worn on its own.

#217440. 15-Minute Evening Yoga to Unwind (That You Can Practice in Bed)

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1420 w)

15-Minute Evening Yoga to Unwind (That You Can Practice in Bed)

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1420 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this short evening yoga routine is designed to help you release stress when you’re ready to wind down for the evening or let go of the day.
  • The stretches are essentially yin yoga poses, except we’re staying in the shapes for less time than the usual 3 to 5 minutes that we expect from yin yoga.
  • Because you’re trying to calm the body and mind, these stretches are not about chasing sensation or pushing yourself into an extreme shape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this short evening yoga routine is designed to help you release stress when you’re ready to wind down for the evening or let go of the day. It brings you a full-body stretch and a lot of relaxation. The poses are all either seated or lying down, so there’s very little effort required. You can even practice the yoga for better sleep routine in bed.

The stretches are essentially yin yoga poses, except we’re staying in the shapes for less time than the usual 3 to 5 minutes that we expect from yin yoga. But these are all poses that you would find in a yin yoga class, so you could stay in any or all of the poses a little longer. The exact 15-minute sequence could be a 75-minute yin yoga class if you have the time or wake up in the middle of the night and are trying to go back to sleep.

Because you’re trying to calm the body and mind, these stretches are not about chasing sensation or pushing yourself into an extreme shape. Try to find a little more ease in each pose as you invite a slower, deeper rhythm to your breath, which signals your nervous system that it’s time to unwind and release. Every time you exhale, see if you can relax a different part of your body and let go of whatever is on your mind from your day.

In a recent development, these stretches are suitable for any experience level. No props are required. Let yourself linger and release into each shape and stay there for 5 to 10 breaths.

It has been revealed that start sitting and then straighten your right leg in front of you. Option one, you can either do your Head to Knee Pose, which we call Half Butterfly in yin yoga, with your left foot to the inside of your thigh.

It has been revealed that option two, you can stretch a little more through the hip and inner thigh if you take your left knee out to the side and your foot behind you with your heel tucked in toward your glutes. If you try option two and you experience any pain or sensitivity in the knee, come back to the first option.

Then start to walk your hands in front of in a forward bend. Let it be a passive stretch, which means you want to let your back round and your head hang. Let gravity do the work for you. Stay here for about 5 breaths or so. While you are in the pose, can you let go of any tension in your arms, jaw, and neck?

Press your hands against the mat and slowly lift yourself back up to sitting.

If it’s not already, bend your left knee out to the side so it’s in line with your left hip. You want to create about a 90-degree bend in your leg and bring your ankle in line with your knee. Then align your right knee so it’s also at a 90-degree angle.

According to recent reports, press your left hip back toward the wall behind you and start to walk your hands back on a diagonal behind you. As soon as you start to feel that sensation through your left hip, pause and breathe into it a little. You can stay propped up on your palms, lower onto your forearms, or lie all the way flat on your back. I’m going to stay propped up on my hands. I find I get the best stretch this way. Breathe here.

Walk your hands in, slowly lifting yourself upright.

According to recent reports, bring your left leg straight in front of you. Cross your left foot over your right thigh, bringing your left foot to the mat outside your right leg. Wrap your right arm around your left and bring your left fingertips to the mat behind you and let them support you. Lift tall through the spine, pressing your shoulders down and away from your ears, then twist toward the left in a Seated Twist. Press into your left big toe and keep both sit bones on the mat. Breathe here.

Then take your Head to Knee or Half Butterfly on the other side, followed by Deer Pose or 90/90 and Seated Twist.

In a recent development, lower all the way down onto your back. Pull your knees toward your chest. Then initiate a little pumping motion. So place your hands on the tops of your knees.

As you inhale, straighten your arms and push your thighs away.

As you exhale, draw your thighs back toward you. Try to relax your legs fully so your arms are controlling the motion. As you do this simple motion, you’re trying to release your lower back muscles as much as possible. You almost want to feel like your legs are moving in water. Take a few more like this.

Recent findings suggest that the next time you bring your knees toward you, widen them toward your shoulders. Either hold here or come into Happy Baby by grabbing hold of your major toes with your two peace fingers, taking your elbows to the insides of your knees, and using your arms to push your legs open a little more. Think of pressing your lower back into the mat, keeping your head and shoulders down on the ground. Sometimes rocking a little side to side can feel really good.

Recent findings suggest that from Happy Baby, keep your right knee close to your chest and extend your left leg straight on the mat to stretch the hip flexors along the front of your left hip. You can take a few ankle rolls with your right foot by making circles, flexing and pointing through your toes, and making any motion through the ankles. Reverse the direction of those circles.

According to recent reports, come into your twist from here, crossing your right leg over your body to the left with the help of your left hand. Stretch your right arm straight out to the side. Think of relaxing your right shoulder down and trying to stack your right hip on top of your left hip.

If you notice yourself obsessing over anything or going over and over a particular thought, just observe what’s happening. Notice that tendency in that pattern, and maybe instead focus on something else that’s a bit more tangible, like the physical sensations in your body from the poses or just the flow of your breath.

Come all the way back to center.

Straighten your right leg any amount, stretching the hamstrings. You can flex and point your foot a couple times.

Then come into Reclined Pigeon Pose by sliding your left foot in, crossing your right ankle over the top of your left knee in a figure-four shape, and reaching your arms along either side of your left leg as you pull your left thigh toward you. Only using a little arm strength. Try to relax your shoulders and keep your head on the  mat. Breathe here.

According to recent reports, keep your left knee drawn toward your chest as you release the pose and extend your right leg straight on the mat. Repeat your ankle rolls, Reclined Twist, and Reclined Pigeon on your left side.

According to recent reports, then you’ll set yourself up for Savasana, your final resting pose. Take up some space with your arms and your legs and then close your eyes. You might do a body scan, bringing your awareness to the crown of your head and slowly working your way down to your fingers and your toes, asking each muscle to relax, to let go, almost as if you could sink into the mat or mattress.

Sources indicate that allow yourself about two minutes here or more if you have the time. Just enjoy the silence and stillness. If you’re already in bed, maybe you stay here.

It has been revealed that start to deepen your breath. Maybe you move your fingers and toes a little. Nice and slow, roll to one side and come to take a seat. Find some length in your spine as you release your shoulders down.

Just pause here. Notice how you feel after just a few minutes of stretching and silence.

Thank you so much, everyone, for doing this short bedtime practice. I hope you feel ready to ease into the rest of your night.

#217438. This Coach’s Fartlek Workout Is One of the Best for Learning a Crucial Running Skill

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1480 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

This Coach’s Fartlek Workout Is One of the Best for Learning a Crucial Running Skill

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1480 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you’re racing your dream marathon or tackling a weekly speed workout, finding the right pace is crucial to your success.
  • It has been revealed that learning to recognize different paces takes practice, run coach Matt Fitzgerald, cofounder of 80/20 endurance, tells Runner’s World.
  • According to recent reports, moving you through several race paces, this workout challenges you to find the subtle differences between them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether you’re racing your dream marathon or tackling a weekly speed workout, finding the right pace is crucial to your success. Go out too hard and you may struggle to hold on. Run too conservatively and you might miss your goal finish.

It has been revealed that learning to recognize different paces takes practice, run coach Matt Fitzgerald, cofounder of 80/20 endurance, tells Runner’s World. One workout he recommends for building this skill is a fartlek he learned from fellow run coach Brad Hudson, his coauthor on the book, Run Faster from the 5K to the Marathon: How to Be Your Own Best Coach.

According to recent reports, moving you through several race paces, this workout challenges you to find the subtle differences between them. The goal? Building both aerobic fitness and a greater sense of pace control.

This workout helps improve your ability to settle into the right effort earlier, as well as enhance your capacity to hold those paces for longer—a perfect session for both optimizing your weekly speed run and helping you run your fastest race.

After an easy running warmup, you’ll run five faster segments, separated by an easy jog of the same duration.

Sources indicate that the base workout uses three target paces: 5K pace for the one-minute segments, 10K pace for the two-minute segments, and half-marathon pace for the three-minute segment. If you don’t know your race paces, you can also go off of rate of perceived exertion (RPE), with 10 equaling all-out effort. You should still be able to have a conversation around 4 RPE.

According to recent reports, fitzgerald indicates the workout should feel “fun hard,” meaning the faster running should feel challenging, but you shouldn’t finish the workout feeling like you just went all out in a race. Each surge is relatively short, so focus on hitting your intended effort rather than pushing as hard as you can.

More experienced, higher-volume runners can extend the pyramid to 1-2-3-2-1-2-3-2-1, again jogging for the same duration after each faster segment. This version includes 17 minutes of faster running and 17 minutes of recovery jogging, compared to just nine minutes of each in the original version.

In Fitzgerald’s experience, many runners tend to think of their effort in two broad categories: slow and fast, but this workout challenges that by demanding more care in differentiating between faster paces.

The one-minute 5K pace efforts should be faster than the two-minute 10K pace efforts, which should be faster than the three-minute half-marathon effort, explains Fitzgerald. The differences between these three paces are small—often just a few seconds per mile—so learning to recognize what each one feels like can help you become a more efficient and more confident runner.

Recent findings suggest that before each segment, think about the effort you’re trying to find. For the first one-minute interval, Fitzgerald suggests literally imagining that you’re starting a 5K race. You wouldn’t want to sprint the opening minute of that race and flame out, so resist that urge here, too.

It has been revealed that try to settle into the right pace by feel, then use your watch to check and adjust. Over time, you’ll grow more attuned to the connection between how you feel and how fast you’re moving. “Your watch can’t [run the workout] for you,” Fitzgerald notes. “It can tell you how fast you’re going. It can’t tell you how fast you should go.”.

Learning to run by feel translates to race day, when you want to hit your goal pace. Your body’s response to the conditions and the effort helps you decide how to proceed through each mile, slowing down or speeding up.

Sources indicate that this workout doesn’t ask you to spend a long time at any single pace. Instead, it gives you short exposures to several intensities within one session.

Hudson, who’s coached multiple Olympians and world-class athletes, tells Runner’s World that moving through a range of paces during a single workout helps with not only pace control, but also running economy or the energy required to run at a given speed.

Sources indicate that additionally, Hudson explains the continuous nature of the fartlek session gives it an aerobic emphasis because you never actually stop running throughout the entirety of the workout. “The faster portions [of the workout] increase oxygen demand, but as you go longer in a workout, the more it becomes aerobic, no matter what,” he indicates. “If you’re keeping the running continuous, the aerobic energy systems just keep going up and up and up.”.

Fitzgerald agrees, although he also notes athletes get some anaerobic stress during the shorter, faster efforts. Think of it as a way to work on several aspects of your fitness at once, rather than a session designed to train just one. Plus, switching between paces can make the workout more mentally engaging than returning to the same effort over and over again.

Sources indicate that the first time you try the workout, you might overshoot a target pace or find it difficult to feel the difference between efforts. That’s okay. Fitzgerald says trial and error is an notable part of developing the skill.

When you repeat the session, look for signs that your pacing is becoming more controlled: You start each segment closer to your intended effort, settle into a steadier rhythm, and maintain a clear difference between your 5K, 10K, and half marathon paces. You may also find it easier to keep your recovery jogs consistent.

Industry observers note that the point is, you don’t need to nail every second of this workout. Learn from your mistakes, adjust when necessary, and remember Fitzgerald’s advice: “Progress over perfection.”.

Industry observers note that it may be tempting to think of the easy jogs simply as passing time between hard segments. But both coaches emphasize the value of continuous running and implore runners not to lose focus during the recovery intervals.

Fitzgerald states teaching your body to recover from a faster effort while still moving presents a unique challenge. Your muscles must learn how to continue producing the energy needed to keep you running efficiently while your body works to recover from the harder interval at the same time. This adaptation translates directly to race day when you have to settle back into race pace after surging to pass another runner or gliding a little too fast down a hill.

According to recent reports, the key is paying attention to how your recovery intervals feel. If you have to slow them down more and more to prepare for the next segment, Fitzgerald notes that may be a sign you’re pushing the faster portions too hard.

The beauty of this workout is if you realize you’ve gone out too quickly, you can easily adjust so you can still complete the workout. If you overcooked one of your speedier segments, Fitzgerald suggests tacking on another minute or so to the easy jog until you breathe easier and lower your heart rate—then adjust your effort level on the next interval.

Because the workout touches several intensity levels, Fitzgerald recommends it during base training or in the off-season. It can help runners maintain well-rounded fitness before they begin building toward a more specific goal.

It can also work as the de facto speed workout during a lighter training week or serve as a secondary quality workout during half-marathon or marathon training. In this case, the session offers a chance to maintain some faster running while the biggest emphasis remains on your long runs and race-specific efforts.

According to recent reports, hudson uses the workout as a key tool in returning to training post-marathon. After a week off, he generally has his athletes begin with easy running. Then, he adds this workout as a way to reintroduce different intensity levels and prepare his athletes for more demanding work ahead.

Whenever you use it, keep its purpose in mind: It’s designed to help you practice changing gears and build general fitness, and using it to support key workouts specifically tailored to your next race makes it even more effective.

Matt Rudisill is an Associate Service Editor who has been with Runner's World since 2025. A Nittany Lion through-and-through, Matt graduated from Penn State in 2022 with a degree in journalism and worked in communications for the university's athletic department for three years as the main contact and photographer for its nationally-ranked cross country and track & field teams. Matt was also heavily involved in communications efforts for Penn State football, men's basketball, and women's gymnastics. In his role with Runner's World, Matt has interviewed Olympians, world champions, and countless experts in the field to create service content that helps runners of all ages and experience levels train smarter and race faster. When he’s not out jogging, Matt can be found tweeting bad takes about the Phillies or watching movies.

Is Your Body Fat Percentage Holding Back Your Cycling Goals? The Answer Depends on Your Age and Ambition.

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For cyclists, body composition is a critical performance factor that goes beyond aesthetics.
  • Industry observers note that understanding age and typical body fat percentage ranges gives us valuable context for setting realistic and healthy body composition goals and determining whether our focus should be on fat loss, strength building, or overall health.
  • 🚴🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For cyclists, body composition is a critical performance factor that goes beyond aesthetics. It directly influences climbing speed, power endurance, and recovery capabilities. Average body-fat percentage averages and recommendations shift as we age depending on individual goals, and whether we’re a recreational rider or a competitive cyclist pursuing maximum power-to-weight ratio.

Industry observers note that understanding age and typical body fat percentage ranges gives us valuable context for setting realistic and healthy body composition goals and determining whether our focus should be on fat loss, strength building, or overall health. (It’s key to note that body fat percentage and BMI (body mass index) are not the same thing.).

🚴🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you? Our Cycling for Weight Loss program will help you find confidence and consistency in your training.

In a recent development, there isn’t a universally “right” body-fat percentage. Ideal targets depend on sex, age, activity level, and specific goals, in addition to whether you’re prioritizing general health, recreational fitness, or competitive performance. However, there are commonly used target ranges per decade that coaches, trainers, and sports scientists use as healthy guidelines (which should be treated as approximate).

Industry observers note that let’s examine “average” body fat percentages guidelines by decade, what the average body fat percentages are for men and women in the United States, and the impact of different measurement methods (DEXA scan, home body fat scale, InBody scan) on results. These averages should be regarded as benchmarks for setting achievable, performance-oriented goals, not as rigid targets. They serve as a navigational tool rather than a mandatory destination.

20s: Competitive athletes: 6–10 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 11–15 percent, Healthy range: 12–20 percent.

30s: Competitive athletes: 7–11 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 12–16 percent, Healthy range: 14–22 percent.

40s: Competitive athletes: 8–12 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 13–17 percent, Healthy range: 16–24 percent.

50s: Competitive athletes: 9–13 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 14–18 percent, Healthy range: 18–26 percent.

60+: Competitive athletes: 10–14 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 15–19 percent, Healthy range: 20–28 percent.

20s: Competitive athletes: 14–18 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 19–23 percent, Healthy range: 20–30 percent.

30s: Competitive athletes: 15–19 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 20–24 percent, Healthy range: 22–32 percent.

40s: Competitive athletes: 16–20 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 21–25 percent, 50s: Competitive athletes: 17–21 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 22–26 percent, Healthy range: 26–36 percent.

60+: Competitive athletes: 18–22 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 23–27 percent, Healthy range: 28–38 percent.

Cyclists specializing in climbing typically aim for the lower end of these ranges, though excessively rapid fat loss can compromise strength and power.

Recent findings suggest that while the ranges above are recommended guidelines, the actual averages for folks according to the CDC look pretty different. The following data on average body fat percentage of men and women in the U. S. has been collected through the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.

Industry observers note that it’s key to note that the body fat percentage measurement method really matters. Home scales that measure body fat percentage can be quite inaccurate according to researchers. In my own experience, an InBody scan (which is the measurement method I recommend for a more reliable assessment, by the way) revealed that my body fat percentage is several percentage points higher than what the home body fat scale I have been testing had measured.

However, even InBody results can fluctuate with hydration levels. DEXA scans offer the most stable results but are generally more expensive. The key is to track trends over time rather than focusing on single numbers.

Industry observers note that when it comes to fat loss, aim for a safe and healthy pace of 0.5-1 percent of body weight per week, while prioritizing preserving lean mass through optimal protein intake and strength training. However, it can be tricky to determine how much of the body weight lost is fat, and factors like how lean someone already is, a person’s metabolism, and training intensity also play a role.

According to recent reports, as an example, in one study of female volunteers on reduced-calorie diets, participants were assigned exercise programs of varying intensity. According to the researchers, the women doing a moderate exercise program lost 6.2 percent body fat over three months on average, which added up to being about 2 percent a month. The intense exercise group lost an average of approximately 10 percent body fat over the same time period, which comes out to around 3.3 percent per month.

Understanding body composition is a valuable tool for cyclists looking to optimize their performance and achieve their goals. By considering your age, sex, activity level, and using reliable measurement methods, you can set realistic targets and tailor your training and nutrition strategies accordingly. Remember, it's all about finding the right balance for your body and your goals.

Natascha Grief is the fitness and reviews editor for Women’s Health. She writes about fitness, health, performance, everyday movement, and the products that help people train and recover better. She brings more than a decade of experience as a NASM-certified personal trainer focused on training women, with specialties in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. She previously worked as the health and fitness editor at Bicycling, and her writing has appeared in Runner’s World and other outlets. Across her work, she’s especially focused on making complex wellness, training, and performance topics approachable and accessible.

#217436. Time Off Feet Will Change How You Think About Recovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1274 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Time Off Feet Will Change How You Think About Recovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1274 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Back when Kerri (Gallagher) Inman was training for professional track races, she told her coach that between runs she would be working as a waitress.
  • In a recent development, now, as a New York City-based TeamRunRun coach, Inman carefully considers her runners’ jobs when creating their training aims.
  • It has been revealed that while time on feet is a metric that many coaches use to quantify a runner’s training volume, few of them use time off feet in a measurable way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back when Kerri (Gallagher) Inman was training for professional track races, she told her coach that between runs she would be working as a waitress. Absolutely not, was his answer. “It’s not as if he would have assigned me a specific time off feet metric,” Inman states, “but my feet needed to rest, and being a waitress was too much time on feet for someone racing the way I did.”.

In a recent development, now, as a New York City-based TeamRunRun coach, Inman carefully considers her runners’ jobs when creating their training aims. For example, a nurse who is “always on her feet,” can’t have runs that overload her so much that she couldn’t keep training or working after a race, Inman states.

It has been revealed that while time on feet is a metric that many coaches use to quantify a runner’s training volume, few of them use time off feet in a measurable way. “We do have an old saying, ‘Never stand when you can sit and never sit when you can lie down,’” says Will Baldwin, USATF and VDOT-certified running coach. Like any generalization, though, that rule isn’t very helpful.

Additionally, despite the many ways runners dig into their metrics and researchers look at small running form and running shoe discrepancies, there is little hard science regarding how much time off your feet you need and how you should best spend that time.

“Instead, you want to use comfort as your paradigm or framework on whether your recovery method is working for you,” says Jim Jastifer, MD, a fellowship-trained orthopedic surgeon specializing in foot and ankle reconstruction with OSMC Orthopedic and Sports Medicine Center in Indiana.

🏃🏻‍♀️The Runner’s World Guide to Recovery is your home for a smarter—from managing soreness and fatigue to easing back into running after a race, offseason, or injury.

In fact, “be comfortable” and “do what makes you happy” may be the best metrics for recovery, according to Jastifer. That’s because it’s not just your feet that need a break—so does your brain.

Are joy and time off feet really related? Turns out, they are. Kara Goucher, distance runner extraordinaire and cohost with Des Linden of the running podcast Nobody Asked Us, has her own way of making sure she gives herself enough time off feet.

Sources indicate that “I love playing Sudoku!” Goucher mentioned on the pod, and she considers her game playing part of her rest and recovery. “It’s time off feet that really does calm my mind and it’s so much better for my brain and mental health than doom scrolling on my phone! It's time to reset my body and my mind.”.

In fact, according to the experts, your goal around recovery and time off feet should be to become self-aware of what your body needs, what your feet need (which may be different than what your larger muscles and soft tissues need), and what your brain needs.

Your feet may actually be the best way to determine how to spend your recovery time; your wearable likely doesn’t correlate its opinion of your recovery to the stress that your feet feel, Jastifer states. “If your Garmin says you’re ready to run, but your feet hurt, you should listen to your feet,” he adds.

Recent findings suggest that “Someone who is running 70/80/100 miles a week isn’t going to recover more by going for a walk,” says Baldwin. This is precisely why Inman’s coach didn’t want her, a professional runner at the time, to add waitressing on top of her training schedule.

“Instead, I try to get my athletes to do low-level movement, such as time on the bike.” For his own time off feet, Baldwin saves his favorite highlights to watch during these sessions so he has less mental taxation.

“Swelling and pain are really the only two reasons you absolutely need to stay off your feet,” states Baldwin. However, you’ll need to be aware of the difference between swelling due to injury and swelling that occurs simply because fluid has gone to your feet because of extensive motion.

“Keeping your feet in motion can actually help swelling,” says Jastifer. Walking can stimulate the movement of blood and lymph (a fluid that carries nutrients to your blood and tissues), which can help recovery, but only if your feet aren’t fighting injury. Signs of injury include pain and discoloration.

Of course, you don’t always have to walk—or do anything with impact—to move your feet. Making circles, rolling a ball under them, or stretching them can reduce the swelling. Again, though, if you feel pain, stop and go to a doctor before you run again.

Percell Dugger, Runna run coach, suggests that you always consider rest and recovery within the context of your training plan, and, if your feet hurt, balance that vital metric against the intensity and effort of a planned workout, even if it’s active recovery.

“In practice and by observation everyone recovers differently,” Inman says. “So, you want to be responsive to whether your feet are telling you they need to rest. If so, maybe get in a pool or get on a bike.”.

Even though there is no clear time or method for recovery, the most notable thing to do between runs is sleep and eat, advises Kristine Sweezey, PT, DPT, CSCS, a physical therapist in Rock Hill, South Carolina, and Charlotte, North Carolina.

Jastifer agrees, adding that rest, cross-training, and time off feet are not at all the same as sleeping. “They serve different functions,” he adds. Without sleep and proper nutrition, athletes cannot actually begin to recover. Moreover, any tricks or tools you use outside of sleep and proper fueling won’t add anything to the recovery equation without a commitment to the basics.

Recent findings suggest that between sleep, time on feet, and time off feet, the experts recommend that you add foot strengthening to your routine. Because improving the abilities of your intrinsic foot muscles will help your feet cope with long and hard miles on the road. So, what are your intrinsic foot muscles? The small muscles that connect within your foot, but not to areas outside of it, such as your Achilles. The muscles in your toes and arch are intrinsic.

“By analogy, we have all the same muscles in our feet that we have in our hands, and while they aren’t significant from a force standpoint, they help regulate the force proprioception in ankle stability and are part of a neuromuscular feedback loop so you don’t have to think about how your feet land which will provide you with stability,” Jastifer says. “If you have foot pain, it might be from these muscles.”.

Sweezey agrees and says you should do all the toe scrunches and toe lifts that you can. “I keep a lacrosse ball under my desk to roll around with my feet,” she says. “It helps decrease the soreness and flushes things out.”.

Finally, when you are ready to get back on the road with your revived feet—whether it’s been a day or a week—make sure you don’t pair two long runs or speed workouts back-to-back, notes Dugger. “Progressive loading is better than high spikes and a dive.” If you and your feet (and your brain) need a break, don’t push too much on your next run.

In a recent development, donna Raskin has had a long career as a health and fitness writer and editor of books and magazine articles. A certified run coach who has practiced yoga for many years, she also loves to lift weights, dance, and go for long walks with her hound dog, Dolly.

Breaking: Garmin LiveTrack Now Alerts Waze Drivers to Nearby Cyclists

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, rearview radars are one of our favorite cycling accessories because they alert riders when a vehicle is approaching from behind.
  • Sources indicate that here’s how it works.
  • In a recent development, waze says the alert comes when a cyclist gets closer, but it hasn’t specified the distance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, rearview radars are one of our favorite cycling accessories because they alert riders when a vehicle is approaching from behind. Now Garmin and Waze are flipping that warning around: Their new partnership alerts drivers when a cyclist using Garmin’s LiveTrack is nearby.

Sources indicate that here’s how it works. Start an outdoor cycling activity with LiveTrack on a compatible Garmin Edge computer or smartwatch, and your location will appear in Waze as a moving cyclist icon. Drivers don’t need to be navigating a route to see cyclists; Waze told me the icons appear whenever the app is open, as riders enter the driver’s broader route area or immediate surroundings.

In a recent development, waze says the alert comes when a cyclist gets closer, but it hasn’t specified the distance. In an email response to my questions, Garmin told me alerts go to “relevant drivers,” usually when the rider and driver are on the same road and traveling in the same direction. A cyclist farther ahead on the driver’s mapped route may also trigger one.

According to recent reports, if several riders are together, Waze shows one icon to avoid repeat alerts. If they spread out, multiple icons appear. Garmin describes the grouping feature as “built-in clustering logic.”.

In a recent development, for Waze owners, cyclist alerts are on by default but can be turned off in the app’s settings. Riders opt in to Waze sharing through Garmin, but only once. After that, sharing starts whenever they begin a cycling LiveTrack, whether they start it manually or set it to start automatically.

Garmin says any Edge computer or smartwatch with LiveTrack is compatible. LiveTrack requires a phone paired with Garmin Connect and cellular coverage; Garmin’s LTE-enabled devices can run LiveTrack without relying on the phone’s connection.

Recent findings suggest that no additional subscription or purchase is required. Waze says drivers see only a temporary alert that a cyclist is nearby, not the rider’s name, identity, or exact route. Sharing stops when the ride ends.

It has been revealed that this is not V2X, the connected-vehicle technology that has been simmering in the background. V2X systems let vehicles exchange information with one another, roadside infrastructure, and other road users, including cyclists. Garmin and Waze are taking an app-based route to a similar goal: LiveTrack sends a rider’s location to Waze, which can alert drivers using the app.

It has been revealed that it’s a sensible idea, but it requires the latest apps and firmware, a Garmin rider who has opted in, a working connection, and a driver using Waze. It isn’t a substitute for cycling-friendly infrastructure, and it won’t fix distracted drivers or jerks in cars. But reminding drivers that cyclists are on the road is a step in the right direction.

Would you enable Waze sharing for your LiveTrack rides? If you use Waze while driving, would a cyclist icon or alert change how you approach the road? Tell us in the comments, or join me on Discord. I’d especially like to hear from riders who already use LiveTrack or Waze: What would you want to know before turning this on?

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

#217434. Is Your AI Strength Plan Wasting Your Time? A Coach Weighs In

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1340 w)

Is Your AI Strength Plan Wasting Your Time? A Coach Weighs In

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1340 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s not uncommon nowadays to ask AI to write your grocery list, design your kid’s birthday party invitation, and advise you on how best to taper before your next race, so we’re fairly certain there are a few triathletes out there asking Claude or Chat to draft a strength training program too.
  • Before you decide to do the same (or perhaps it’s too late and you already have), we thought we’d run an AI experiment where we ask a real human strength coach to assess the bot’s work to help decide how much of the strategy is helpful for a multisport athlete, and how much would be a waste of time.
  • We asked ChatGPT for a strength routine suitable for a triathlete, and about four seconds later it returned a two-day plan complete with sets and reps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete).

It’s not uncommon nowadays to ask AI to write your grocery list, design your kid’s birthday party invitation, and advise you on how best to taper before your next race, so we’re fairly certain there are a few triathletes out there asking Claude or Chat to draft a strength training program too.

Before you decide to do the same (or perhaps it’s too late and you already have), we thought we’d run an AI experiment where we ask a real human strength coach to assess the bot’s work to help decide how much of the strategy is helpful for a multisport athlete, and how much would be a waste of time.

We asked ChatGPT for a strength routine suitable for a triathlete, and about four seconds later it returned a two-day plan complete with sets and reps.

Day one covered the lower body and core: squats or goblet squats, Romanian deadlifts, reverse lunges, standing calf raises, dead bugs, and side planks.

Recent findings suggest that day two went after the upper body and posterior chain: dumbbell bench press or push-ups, rows, lat pulldowns or assisted pull-ups, single-leg Romanian deadlifts, glute bridges or hip thrusts, and Pallof presses. The prescription included three sets of 8-10 reps, for 40 to 50 minutes per session, to be followed for 8-12 weeks.

According to recent reports, it all looked perfectly sensible and not too dissimilar to what many triathletes do in most strength workouts. But for a triathlete who’s already squeezing three sports into one week, strength workouts should really be periodized and designed to augment what’s happening in the triathlete’s sport-specific training life (and the off-season is the one time of year when it’s great to do more in the gym, not less).

So with this in mind, we handed the plan to strength coach Sam Hengehold, who works with triathletes of all ages and abilities at Kinesis Integrated Performance in Boulder, Colorado. “I’d argue it is not right, but it’s also not wrong,” she notes. “The plan is general, but it is not beneficial.”.

Here’s the surprise: Hengehold wouldn’t strike a single exercise from the list.

“All exercises listed are actually great and could very well be integrated into a triathlete strength routine,” she says. “The limiter here is the lack of periodization and volume/load variables.”.

Two of ChatGPT’s picks earn special praise:.

Calf raises: “Many triathletes miss this integral exercise in their strength routine,” Hengehold says. “Lower leg injuries are extremely common with triathletes.” As a general rule, Hengehold wants athletes working toward calf raises at 1.5 times their body weight to build resiliency against injury in the calf, ankle, and foot.

According to recent reports, glute bridges: “A safe way to build power for beginners in strength training,” Hengehold says. They mostly train the glutes and core, the muscle groups that underpin all three disciplines.

So if the exercises are fine, where does the wasted time come in? It’s in how the initiative asks you to do them.

To its credit, ChatGPT suggests lifting less often as race day approaches and adding a little load once the sets feel solid. But the exercises, sets, and reps never change. Your swim, bike, and run training is built in cycles around your races, and Hengehold advises that your lifting should be too.

In a recent development, in the off-season, strength work can take priority and endurance training becomes the base. In race season, that flips: Lifting is there to support your swim, bike, and run, and to keep your body resilient. A strategy that looks identical in January and July does neither job well.

“Over time, it will just be an energy suck of a session, causing more fatigue in the athlete with minimal benefit,” Hengehold warns.

Industry observers note that chatGPT’s warm-up gets one line: 5-10 minutes of easy cardio, mobility, and lighter practice sets. Hengehold wants something more deliberate, with activation work chosen to prepare you for the main lift of the day.

According to recent reports, “Warm-up and activation encourages proper form and oils the muscles,” Hengehold says. “Typically, that would include some sort of dynamic stretching, mobility, or preparation exercise that will aid in the main lift goals of the session. Before squats, for example, that might mean 90/90 hip rotations for hip mobility and banded clamshells to wake up the gluteus medius.” This matters if you want to avoid injury and get the most from every rep.

The substantial, complex lifts belong at the start of the session, when you’re fresh and can control your form. They also work better when paired with an athletic movement, Hengehold notes, so the brain learns what the strength is for.

Recent findings suggest that follow loaded squats with box jumps, for instance, and you reinforce the power you need at toe-off on the run or when pushing watts on the bike. ChatGPT’s plan has no jumps and no explosive work at all.

“Neuromuscular understanding and adaptation is absolutely necessary for triathletes to maximize the benefit of strength training,” Hengehold says. Without it, you get some injury prevention and extra muscle mass, but not much else.

Hengehold named three categories of strength work that matter most for triathletes:.

Recent findings suggest that core work: Think isometric holds and slow, controlled movements, with deep breathing throughout, to work the transverse abdominal muscles. Hengehold’s picks: planks with alternating shoulder taps, dead bugs, and bird dogs.

In a recent development, unilateral movements: Single-leg Romanian deadlifts, Bulgarian split squats, front-foot elevated reverse lunges, and single-leg calf raises all make each side do its own share of the work. Swimming, biking, and running give a stronger side plenty of chances to cover for a weaker one, and these exercises help break those overcompensation patterns.

Squat variations: Isometric squats (holding the position) and eccentric squats (slowing the lowering phase) are a safe way to build resilience in the lower body and core. The squat is also endlessly adjustable, so it can be tweaked to target whatever you need most.

What you lift, and how, should depend on how far you are from your next race.

Far from race day: This is the time for heavy strength training alongside base swim, bike, and run work. Make complex lifts the centerpiece. Hengehold likes the trap bar deadlift. Get the form and technique down first, then spend a block (typically four to six weeks) building a base with high reps and low weight. Take a deload week, then switch to low reps and heavy weight to build real strength and durability.

Recent findings suggest that in race season: Triathlon training takes over, and strength work drops to maintenance. Unilateral exercises move to the front, scheduled closely around your key sessions and races. Reps and load should go mostly on perceived effort and how you’re feeling, physically and emotionally. Hengehold also stresses mobility work, foam rolling, and stretching during this period.

One last thing no chatbot can do is look at your form. If you’re new to the weight room, Hengehold recommends having a gym friend or personal trainer check your technique early on: “Bad habits are hard to break and cause damage over time, and the same is true with your swimming, biking, and running.”.

Yet technique is only part of what a generic strategy misses.

“Triathletes are some of the most hardworking individuals on the planet and managing training, fatigue, and recovery requires extreme attention to detail,” Hengehold indicates. “The time, energy, and hard work need to be maximized to be worth it, which means a generalized strength plan will not meet the standard. Each athlete is a unique individual with individual needs that require an individualized plan.”.

Recent findings suggest that none of this is an argument against strength training — far from it. Hengehold calls it “absolutely essential to longevity in sport and health” and recommends it for every athlete. The argument is against spending your limited time and energy on a initiative that wasn’t written with you in mind.

Recent findings suggest that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 19, 2026: Black Friday sales are in full swing. Several of our already low-priced trainers are discounted for as high as 30% off, including our Best Overall, the New Balance 680v9.

“All you need is a pair of shoes to start running” isn’t exactly truthful. If you hate your toenails and heels, by all means, wear Converse high-tops. A good pair of running shoes will spare your digits and the skin on your feet—but that doesn’t mean you have to drop cash on expensive trainers.

Cheap running shoes, models less than $130, are a respectable choice for beginners and vets wanting to save. From plush to moderately cushioned, we’ve listed affordable running shoes on this list that’ll help you save up for more run gear, like a fancy GPS watch or that next destination race.

In a recent development, to find the best shoes under $130, we performed comprehensive research on top-rated trainers by well-known brands, and called in shoes for our shoe program testers and staff to evaluate. These shoes were vetted by scrutinizing fit, ride, and comfort. To give you both options, we included our premium recommendation for each shoe from our Best Running Shoes buying guide, just in case you want to spend some extra cash.

🏃 For even more choices, head to The Best Running Shoes of 2026.

We also spoke with Footwear Buyer Jon Notary, who works at the local running store Aardvark Sports Shop in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania. Notary provides insight on what you’re compromising on when buying cheap shoes, and gives advice on what to look for when you’re out shopping for your next pair.

Sources indicate that buying an affordable trainer doesn’t necessarily mean subpar features. Brands will sometimes incorporate “old” technology into these shoes, like midsole foams, to mitigate a high price. But you are sacrificing some premium specs, like plush cushioning and more durable materials.

Below is a comparison chart of our Best Overall budget trainer, the Newly introduced Balance Fresh Foam 680v9, versus the brand’s premium daily trainer, the Fresh Foam X 880v15. The latter has the next generation of Fresh Foam, Fresh Foam X, and more cushioning. You save almost half the money with the 680v9, but you get what you paid for with the 880v15.

The 680v9 is still a reliable shoe for everyday runs and light workouts. If you’re an efficient runner (you don’t wear down your shoes’ soles faster than the average runner), you may even get more mileage out of the 680v9s. It comes down to what you’re willing to give up and what you’re willing to spend.

Recent findings suggest that all the trainers on this list are Best Value material, but the 680v9 deserves the title for its consistency with each revision. Though not as plush or responsive as, say, the more expensive 1080 or 880, the 680 still encapsulates New Balance’s soft-cushioned feel, absorbing shock and promoting comfort on every run.

In a recent development, its Fresh Foam midsole provides a supportive, plush, lightweight ride, making the 680v9 an excellent choice as an everyday trainer that can handle base-building mileage. A breathable, cozy upper makes this a comfy running shoe and great for casual wear, as well.

You can’t go wrong with the Launch 12 for a speed shoe, especially when it has DNA Flash v2, the foam featured in the Hyperion Elite 4. The nitrogen-infused supercritical foam is lightweight and responsive; it provides plenty of pop for fast workouts on the road and track.

One drawback, at least for runners with wide feet, is that the midfoot area is quite narrow.

In a recent development, “No matter how many times I loosened and re-laced my shoes, it always felt too tight through the midfoot area, causing some noticeable discomfort,” stated RW editor Ashley Tysiac. “While I can appreciate its secure fit, I think this system could have been reimagined to be a bit more forgiving in that area to provide more comfort.”.

Despite her distaste for the Launch 12’s tightness, she praised the shoe’s lightweight and responsiveness. Tysiac found the shoe’s simplicity refreshing in our max-cushioned era of trainers.

“I think the weight of the shoe is the best part, as it’s very light yet provides a pretty stable ride,” she said. “That made it the perfect shoe for runs where I wanted to pick up the pace a bit without being dragged down by heavy shoes, and even a good option for those recovery days when I still wanted to feel light on my feet while running at a slower pace.”.

It has been revealed that 👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best Overall Shoe → Adidas Adizero Evo SL (Men’s/Women’s).

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com.

The GT-1000 15 provides stability without overbearing, rigid foam pieces, or a high price tag. The shoe has Asics’s 3D Guidance System, which uses a broader platform and reshaping in the heel and forefoot to help with inward foot rolling.

The shoe has high-abrasion Ahar rubber that can withstand aggressive gait patterns and provide reliable traction on slippery surfaces and sharp corners. The fit is slightly narrower than past models, so you may want to size up.

The shoe is also great for long runs thanks to its PureGel tech and FF Blast midsole; you’ll have a soft ride that absorbs impact.

Sources indicate that 👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best Stability Shoe → Brooks Adrenaline GTS 26 (Men’s/Women’s).

Recent findings suggest that the FloatZig 2 looks bulky with its unconventional, zigzag midsole rim around the shoe. But we found it surprisingly lightweight during testing. Its soft cushioning—that midsole isn’t just for looks—provided a supportive bed for testers’ feet.

“What I found most enjoyable about this shoe was how lightweight and balanced it is,” remarked tester Mike Parmer. “The fit and comfort allowed longer training runs and no sore feet or toes. This shoe is one of the better shoes I have tested recently and would compare equally to Hoka.”.

The Superfloat+ midsole promotes high energy return, giving a much-needed boost when the road feels long.

In a recent development, 👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best for Shock Absorption Shoe → Upcoming Balance 1080v15 (Men’s/Women’s).

Industry observers note that anta proves you can have premium cushioning on a budget. The PG7 3 has an incredibly plush feel, making the shoe versatile for easy runs, long runs, and casual wear. The cushioning stays soft and also supportive, allowing you to run hard and fast.

In my runs in the PG7 3, I’ve found the ride and feel comparable to the Saucony Triumph and Brooks Glycerin.

Industry observers note that “Budget shoes always feel cheap,” noted Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate. “There’s an undeniable compromise you have to make to pay less. And that stinks. In this case, the PG7 doesn’t really feel like it’s holding anything back. It’s comfortable, cushioned, and supportive. It’s going to work as a daily driver for a lot of runners.”.

👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best for Long Runs Shoe → Nike Structure Plus (Men’s/Women’s).

Though the C202 7 costs the most on this list, it’s more than worth the $130 price. Compared to racing shoes that are upward of $200, the C202 7 has a full-length carbon-fiber plate sandwiched in its midsole of DAN cushioning, a TPU supercritical foam.

Industry observers note that the shoe feels snappy and responsive. And it has good traction too. Furrer tested the shoe during a rainy 5K in San Antonio, Texas. While other competitors wiped out on slick turns, Furrer stayed vertical cutting corners and accelerating on waterlogged sidewalks and muddy dividers.

Industry observers note that 👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best for Racing Marathons Shoe → Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s).

Recent findings suggest that trail running demands a lot from your shoes. Between the hard-charging descents and scraping against rough rocks, the last thing you want is a cheap, flimsy shoe that won’t hold up. The Saucony Excursion TR17 has Versarun, which absorbs impact and provides comfy cushioning over trail debris.

One knock is the shoe is quite heavy, and it runs a little small and narrow, so consider sizing up and trying on the wide version.

All models of the Excursion TR17 have 4.5mm lugs to keep you on your toes when things get dicey.

According to recent reports, 👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best for Trails Shoe → Hoka Speedgoat 7 (Men’s/Women’s).

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

According to Notary, the two main sacrifices you make when buying cheaper running shoes are comfort and longevity. That doesn’t mean you’re stuck with choosing uncomfortable shoes when you’re searching for cheaper pairs. It just means you have to do the extra, er, footwork, when considering more affordable shoes.

Notary notes the materials are not as premium or as durable. “That being stated, the industry does benefit from what I call the technology trickle-down; many of the materials on lower priced models were once used on a ‘fancier’ one.” For example, the Brooks Launch 12 has DNA Flash v2 foam which was used in its Hyperion Elite super shoes.

“A lower cost shoe will use older foams and fabrics, possibly less outsole, or no outsole, and less involved construction techniques. All of those realities typically lead to less overall comfort than what else is right now available,” indicates Notary. A cheaper shoe will be comfortable, it just won’t have the same max plush and support of a top-shelf trainer.

According to recent reports, notary states comfort is king. “If it feels heavy, stiff, and firm in the store, don’t expect that to change. Conversely, if it feels hyper-light, super flexible, and marshmallowy soft, there is a good chance it won’t be as durable.”.

Perhaps you’re leaning toward one end of the spectrum of cushioning or somewhere in the middle. The best way to find if a cheap shoe—or any running shoe—is right for you is to try it on first and go for a test run in the store. Some shoe stores allow you to run on the sidewalk or on a treadmill to see if the shoe’s a good fit.

In a recent development, cheap running shoes have a shorter shelf life. “Because the materials are less premium they typically break down faster even when they’re not being worn,” notes Notary. “This isn’t always true and is somewhat of a generalization, but higher grade materials generally offer more durability. If we’re considering mileage, a lower-cost shoe typically yields fewer miles.”.

Notary adds, however, that some of the most expensive running shoes on the market right now, i.e., super shoes or shoes with a carbon plate, also have a shorter mileage life, which is another thing to put in perspective.

Sources indicate that we took pains not to include discounted models on this list but shouldn’t be overlooked when buying running shoes. In some cases, the differences between last season and the current season are unnoticeable.

When the Price Is Too Good to Be True.

Beware of dupes on sites like Amazon. A usually expensive model slapped with a too-good-to-be-true price tag is probably just that. The model in question likely isn’t the shoe promised, is poorly made, and could cause injury due to poor quality materials. Check the seller to see it’s from the actual brand (and make sure it’s not someone posing as a well-known brand).

It has been revealed that for models by lesser known brands, Notary gives us some pointers when choosing running shoes. “Things to look for are a rubber outsole and a removable footbed/liner,” he claims. “These are two quick check aspects of a viable running shoe. Also, look for fewer sewn overlays on the upper, more will only cause problems with flexibility and add excessive weight to the shoe.”.

Will cheap running shoes make me run slower?

According to recent reports, in general, a cheaper shoe will not have as much pop or energy return as a more expensive one which in theory should make it slower. Lower cost shoes will likely lack plating or supercritical foams found in today’s ‘fastest’ shoes. However, a lot depends on how comfortably the shoe moves with you. Some of the ‘fastest’ shoes on the market today don’t agree with my body’s mechanics, and I find them slower than more conventional shoes in my rotation.

Are cheap running shoes a good choice for new runners?

Recent findings suggest that in my world, any shoe that gets someone running is a good choice. That noted, a well-fitting, comfortable technical running shoe will have a much better chance of keeping a newly introduced runner in the sport.

It’s a shame that with so much great and relatively affordable product available, many people start the sport in the wrong shoe and quit, never knowing a different reality exists for them. Unfortunately the ‘running shoe’ category is a bit of a catch-all, and there are plenty of shoes categorized as ‘running’ that have no place being labeled as such.

How old can a past shoe model be for it to be ok to run in?

Unworn shoes will definitely lose some cushioning after about two to five years due to oxidization, which hardens the midsole foam. Glue also weakens over time, increasing the risk of delamination in shoes that have been sitting around a while, primarily between the upper and the midsole and the midsole and the outsole. They can be used, sure, but they won’t have the typical 300 to 500 mile range of usability nor the comfort of a ‘fresher’ pair.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#217432. What the Full Moon in Gemini Means for You

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2332 w)
