What the Full Moon in Gemini Means for You

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2332 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are breakthroughs, large and small, awaiting you on the full Moon in Gemini.
  • The Moon reaches its fullest light on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, at 6:54 am PT.
  • Gemini is the sign of the twins, ruled by the planet Mercury and the element of air.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are breakthroughs, large and small, awaiting you on the full Moon in Gemini. Insights that have the power to change everything can arrive in an instant. A sentence you have repeated to yourself for years might suddenly sound false. A thought that once felt like a fact might reveal itself as a fear. You might hear yourself say something about your life and realize, in the middle of saying it, that you no longer believe it. It’s a powerful supermoon, one designed to help you release what no longer belongs to you.

The Moon reaches its fullest light on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, at 6:54 am PT.

Gemini is the sign of the twins, ruled by the planet Mercury and the element of air. It moves rapidly, influencing our intellect and communication and touching our minds, our nervous systems, our voices, and the way we take in and share information. Gemini is the part of us that asks questions, makes connections, strikes up a conversation with a stranger, and wants to know a little about everything. It is curiosity in motion.

The twins also represent duality. Gemini reminds us that we are complex, that we can hold two feelings at once, and that life is rarely black or white. There are shades of gray everywhere, and within that uncertainty exists endless possibility.

Sources indicate that gemini is the voice in your head that narrates your day. It names what is happening to you, decides what it means, and tells you what to expect next. This voice speaks to you more than any other person in your life. It is there when you wake up and when you fall asleep. It comments on your work, your relationships, and your decisions. It is the stories you live by. Most of the time, you do not even notice it is speaking. It feels less like a voice and more like the truth.

But it is a voice. And a voice can change.

Think about where your inner voice came from. Some of it is yours, formed through your own experience and your own knowing. Some of it was inherited. A parent’s worry. A teacher’s doubt. A sentence someone said to you once, at the wrong moment, that you have been repeating to yourself ever since. Some of it came from society, from every message that told you who you were supposed to be and how much you were allowed to want. Over the years, all of these voices blended into one, and you started to call it you.

Sources indicate that the words you use about yourself become the life you live. If your inner voice tells you something is not possible, you stop reaching for it. You do not apply, you do not ask, you do not try, and the life that follows proves the voice right. But when the voice changes, the reaching changes. And when the reaching changes, the life changes. A newly introduced inner voice is how you begin to believe what is possible.

There is science behind this. Research on moments of insight, those sudden aha experiences, reveals that they tend to arrive when we’re in a less-anxious state of mind rather than straining for an answer. The brain makes surprising connections when we stop gripping the problem. This full Moon asks you to slow down, breathe, and loosen your hold on the old voice before reaching for the latest one. The breakthrough comes more easily when you make space for it.

Gemini is also one of the most social signs of the zodiac, and that is part of the medicine. Sometimes the new voice arrives through someone else. A friend reflects you back to yourself in a way you never considered. A stranger notes the exact sentence you needed. A line in a book or a song lands differently than it ever has before. Be open to these messages. Stay curious. Talk to people. Listen more than usual. The universe often delivers our breakthroughs through the voices of others.

It has been revealed that on the full Moon in Gemini, let yourself be curious about your own mind. Listen to the voice in your head as if you were hearing it for the first time. Notice what it says. Notice whose voice it sounds like. And then notice the quieter voice underneath, the one that has always believed in you. That is the voice that is ready to rise.

As the Moon in Gemini finds itself opposite the Sun in Sagittarius, we can experience the illumination of both signs. Of all the opposing signs of the zodiac, Gemini and Sagittarius are the most alike. Both are in search of truth. Both follow their curiosity wherever it leads. Both love to learn, explore, and share what they discover. Gemini occupies the third house of communication and the immediate world around us. Sagittarius occupies the ninth house of truth, philosophy, and the wider world. Together they form the axis of the mind.

It has been revealed that gemini sees the details. Sagittarius sees the massive picture. Gemini collects the individual pieces of information. Sagittarius weaves them into meaning. Gemini asks what is happening. Sagittarius asks why. Together they give us a complete view of how we think.

It has been revealed that this year, there is another way to see this axis. Gemini is the voice. Sagittarius is the belief.

Your beliefs are the things you hold to be true about life, about yourself, and about what is possible. They shape everything. But beliefs are not built in a single day. They are built, sentence by sentence, from the words you hear and repeat. Every time your inner voice claims something, it adds to a belief. Say “things never work out for me” enough times and it becomes a philosophy. Say “something good is always on its way” enough times and that becomes a philosophy, too.

This is the gift of the Gemini and Sagittarius opposition on this full Moon. When the voice changes, the belief follows. As you release the old voice and let the upcoming one rise, you are not only changing your thoughts. You are rebuilding what you believe is possible for your life. And Sagittarius, ruled by Jupiter, the planet of expansion, gives that belief room to become as big as your life is meant to be.

With the full Moon, we have the opportunity to release the lower vibrations of these signs and integrate the higher ones.

Recent findings suggest that gemini’s lower vibration highlights up as scattered thinking and division. In this frequency, the mind races. We jump from thought to thought without landing anywhere. We talk more than we listen. We overshadow other people’s truth to prove our own knowledge. We get lost in the details, in the noise, in the endless information coming at us, and we lose the thread of what we actually feel. We might repeat the same anxious story over and over, and each time it gets louder. Gemini’s low side can also look like gossip, overthinking, and indecision, where two voices inside us argue and neither one wins.

According to recent reports, if you find yourself in the lower vibration of Gemini, slow down. Take a long, slow breath and bring yourself back into your body. Spend more time listening than talking. When you notice the mind racing, ask yourself one simple question. What is true right now? Then let the rest go quiet.

According to recent reports, sagittarius has a lower vibration, too. It looks like certainty. In this frequency, we believe we already have all the answers. We become self righteous about our views and close ourselves off to anything that challenges them. We forget that everyone has something to teach us. Sagittarius’s low side can also show up as restlessness and always chasing the next horizon instead of arriving where we are. Sometimes it looks like the opposite of faith. It can be a belief that life is working against us, held just as tightly as any other philosophy.

Recent findings suggest that if you find yourself in the lower vibration of Sagittarius, get curious about a perspective that is different from yours. Ask yourself which of your beliefs you chose and which you simply inherited. Release your need to be right. This is your permission to change your mind about your own life.

When we align with the higher vibrations of both signs, Gemini gives us a voice that is curious, open, and kind. Sagittarius gives us a belief that is expansive and full of faith. They create someone who speaks to themselves like a trusted friend, who believes in what is possible, and who is always willing to learn. We understand the details of what is needed to create our intentions, and we hold the vision of where we are headed.

The highest merger of these energies teaches us that there is no you or me. There is only us. Every voice we hear, every story we are told, every conversation we have is part of one great exchange. When we open our minds to one another, the messages we need find us at just the right time.

In a recent development, each full Moon carries its own astrological fingerprint, with other cosmic bodies forming their own conversations on that day. These conversations are called aspects, and they add layers of meaning to the full Moon. Some create tension. Others create flow. Together they shape the emotional landscape you are working with. On the full Moon in Gemini, the story of the aspects is one of support.

Recent findings suggest that the entire axis of this full Moon is charged with Uranus. The Moon reaches its fullest light in Gemini. Just over one degree away sits Uranus. The Moon and Uranus are conjunct, which means they share the same part of the sky and blend their energies together. The next afternoon, the Sun reaches its exact opposition to Uranus.

Uranus is the planet of awakening. It rules sudden insight, liberation, innovation, and the unexpected. It is the flash of lightning that lights up an entire landscape in an instant, revealing what was there all along. Uranus breaks patterns. It frees us from whatever has become too small, too rigid, or too old for who we are becoming. Its gifts often arrive promptly, and sometimes they are a surprise. But they always move us toward more liberation and more truth.

Uranus entered Gemini on April 26, 2026, the first time it was in this sign since the 1940s. Out in the world, Uranus in Gemini is sparking a revolution in communication, technology, and the way we learn and share information. Within each of us, it is sparking a revolution in the way we speak to ourselves.

Industry observers note that right now, Uranus is retrograde. It stationed retrograde on September 10, 2026, in Gemini and will station direct on February 8th, 2027, in Gemini. When a planet is retrograde, its energy turns inward. So the breakthrough of this full Moon is not about what you say out loud to the world. It is about what you say to yourself. With Uranus sitting beside it, Gemini’s speed meets Uranus’s suddenness, and that combination is powerful.

It has been revealed that this full Moon in Gemini also a Supermoon. A Supermoon happens when the Moon reaches its fullest light near perigee, which is the closest point to the Earth in its orbit. It appears larger and brighter than usual as it rises. Energetically, a Supermoon amplifies everything influenced by the full Moon. Emotions feel bigger. Insights land with more force. Release runs deeper. With Uranus sitting right beside the Moon, the breakthrough with your inner voice is turned all the way up.

It has been revealed that this year, the Sun also forms a trine to Neptune in Aries, a harmonious connection between our sense of self and our dreams. Neptune adds faith, vision, and imagination to this opposition. It helps Sagittarius believe in something bigger than what it can see. It softens the edges of the old voice and makes room for the dream underneath it. As you work with the full Moon in Gemini, let yourself imagine. Let yourself dream bigger than feels reasonable. Neptune is helping you see a life your old voice never had words for.

Sources indicate that there is a voice that speaks to you more than any other. It is with you in the shower and in the car, in meetings and in quiet moments, when you look in the mirror and when you lie awake at night. It is the voice in your own head. Most of us never stop to question it. We assume that what it says is simply true.

But this voice was shaped over a lifetime, by experiences, by people, by pain, and by the world around us. Some of what it claims is wise. Some of it is love. And some of it is old, outdated, and borrowed from people who did not know who you would become.

This full Moon in Gemini, with Uranus sitting beside it, is your opportunity to hear that voice clearly and to choose a fresh one. A voice that believes in you. A voice that can carry you into 2027 and help you see what is possible for your life.

The changes this full Moon brings are meant to free you, not to shake you apart. Let the old voice go. Listen for the new one. It has been waiting for you. So step outside on the evening of the full Moon in Gemini and look up as it rises. Let the size of that Moon remind you how major your life is allowed to be.

The 10 Best Sports Bras for Running, Tested for High-Impact Support

  • And yes, we look at bras with and without pads, because anyone who has ever wrestled with those flimsy things can tell you that while they may hide the headlights, there are times when you’d rather light them on fire than deal with them before lacing up and hitting your run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that nothing sucks harder on a run than an uncomfortable, unsupportive (or too supportive) sports bra that digs, chafes, causes pools of sweat to collect, and generally makes you curse the day you hit puberty. Luckily, we’re looking out for you. Our team was as rigorous with bras as we are with running shoes, treadmills, and other gear as we evaluated them. We focused chiefly on comfort, breathability, durability, the potential to chafe, bounce control, and ease of laundering.

And yes, we look at bras with and without pads, because anyone who has ever wrestled with those flimsy things can tell you that while they may hide the headlights, there are times when you’d rather light them on fire than deal with them before lacing up and hitting your run.

The best sports bras for running work with your cup and band size, what level of support you require, and how you like it to fit on your frame. We chose a range of adjustable high-impact bras, traditional pullover sports bras, bras with pockets, bras that are budget-friendly, and bras made for different size and shape breasts.

Recent findings suggest that our testers span all experience levels, paces, ages, and body types, with sizes ranging from 28 to 40 bands and A to F cups. Over the past year, we’ve tested more than 45 different sports bras to see how they held us and how they held up. We wore these bras for running plus low- to high-intensity workouts like yoga and HIIT, evaluating each for comfort, breathability, mobility, and—of course—support.

We sorted our picks into three categories: adjustable bras (hook-and-eye closures, zip fronts, Velcro, or adjustable straps), pullover bras (no adjusting required, though maybe some contorting), and pocket bras, which we also rank on storage space and how packing affects mobility and support.

We revision this roundup regularly, but inventory changes fast—some colors and sizes may run low.

There are few bras that you try on and feel comfortable straight out of the bag, but the Run Times Bra manages. It’s a comfortably compressive, encapsulated, adjustable bra that is designed to take you for long miles. It has sweat-wicking fabric that prevents pooling under the breasts, and the mesh panel at the top allows for additional breathability. On a long run, that extra breeze makes a huge difference in comfort and chafing prevention.

In a recent development, our tester took this out on a 35-mile climbing trail run through the Adirondack Mountains and through the heat and the rain. The bra performed beautifully, even under a long-sleeve tee and tech jacket. It didn’t get swampy, nor did the shirt start to stick to it, as can happen when sweat and water soak a T-shirt.

It’s especially great for women who have lost a significant amount of breast volume due to weight loss or breastfeeding because of how the additional Lycra material encapsulates and hugs each breast. Where some bras may make these breasts feel almost “folded,” the Run Times Bra simply supports and cradles your breasts in an anatomically comfortable way.

Old Navy has long been a favorite of ours for its inexpensive athletic wear, and now, that also includes sports bras. The PowerSoft bra hits well outside of its weight class in both features and performance, starting with a front zipper that spares you the post-run wrestle of a sweaty pullover. Adjustable cross-back straps let you fix the fit through your shoulders and torso, and the brand’s namesake PowerSoft fabric is buttery soft with moisture-wicking that holds up when you’re hitting those hot runs.

Sources indicate that the size range is where Old Navy really shows up the competition: broader than what many premium brands offer. At $40 full price—and often marked down below $25—it’s impossible to overlook.

And not for anything, this is one of the bras we tested with a zipper that isn’t a sensory nightmare for our autistic testers.

Sources indicate that the construction of this bra makes it among the best I’ve ever worn. The uniqueness of that construction? A dual adjustable strap in the back that allows you to dial in your fit. If you need more support up top, you can clasp it closer together. Need a bit more band space? The lower hooks are there for you. This is a bra designed for women who may have volume in different spots across their ribs and chest. And it works beautifully.

Industry observers note that the construction also makes for a more comfortable experience. I have a pretty severe rib flare thanks to pregnancy and a short waist, and the ability to tighten the bra more up on top and less on the bottom makes it comfier than most other bras I’ve tested.

However, if you have pronounced lat muscles, you may notice a bit of rubbing during pull-ups because of where the shoulder straps fall. But that nitpicky aspect doesn’t take away from it being an all-around winner.

Runderwear Power Running Bra Review.

According to recent reports, the Shadowlite is very sensory friendly. The flat-locked seams are coated and stitched in a way that they don’t rub or interfere with your run. It’s also not a traditional encapsulation bra, nor is it a traditional pullover compression bra. Instead, it’s a combination of the two. Instead of the sewn-in lifting panel squeezing the breasts together and in, it lifts them together without the squish.

Recent findings suggest that “The bra gave me a very secure feeling without restricting my breathing—I forgot I was wearing it, which is always the best possible outcome,” remarked Senior Features Editor Pavlína Černá. “The band has ribbing on the inside that I found helpful in keeping the bra in place—no feeling of rotation on the run. I usually try to get two runs out of a bra, if I can, before washing. I was able to do three with this bra.”.

Sources indicate that the gel-cushioned straps on this sports bra ensure you won’t get raw markings from all-day wear and intense activities. The Spot Comfort is also extremely breathable and moisture-wicking—mesh on the adjustable straps and front panel promotes ventilation.

In a recent development, the bra is lined with molded cups for non-underwire support, and the back hook-and-eye closure makes it easy to take the bra off. One thing to consider: size up. We found the fit a little too snug, even on the loosest hook-and-eye setting. It’s also H-back-only, which may not be everyone’s preference when wearing a sports bra. This one launders like a dream—seriously. For the price, it doesn’t pill, it doesn’t stretch out, and we don’t always follow our own laundering advice and just throw it in with everything and call it good.

Sources indicate that the Energy’s foam cups, which go up to size DDD, offer comfortable and secure support while also providing a flattering fit that doesn’t squish the chest down. In the back, we appreciate the crisscross straps’ fun design as well as their functionality—once adjusted, the straps stay in place for a no-budge run.

According to recent reports, some of our testers reported that the Energy runs small, so it may be best to order a size up to ensure the bra is a good fit or try it on in person. This bra also has three points of adjustment: the chest band as well as both sets of cross straps.

The bra that underwent 2,000-plus miles of ultrarunning is buttery soft and has plenty of lift. Tested during lululemon’s Further campaign, in which 10 women runners ran an ultra over the course of six days, the Go Further Bra is a high-impact pullover that can carry you through thousands of miles—and it doesn’t have to be in one go.

According to recent reports, the bra is made of lululemon’s Ultralu fabric, which feels yoga legging smooth. Support Code technology in the cups changes the stiffness of the cups to prevent your breasts from bouncing as you run. You can see the tech when the bra is on a flat surface; instead of the conical domes you see on an encapsulation bra, the cups pucker and look slightly sunken in.

Our tester, who wears a 32B and tested the Go Further in a small, had her doubts when she saw the bra lying flat on her desk. She changed her mind after running in the Go Further. “From the look of her, I was convinced that she would never fit, and that she’s made for much bigger boobs than mine,” she indicates. “And was I wrong! She fits like a glove and is easy to put on and take off. She doesn’t deprive me of air but is completely supportive on my runs.”.

You’ve probably seen influencer ads for this all over your social media feeds. Running Girl’s ad budget is thriving, but thankfully, your budget will be too, if you grab this one. The bra is comfortably high-impact with no squish. Instead, the molded cups lift and separate your breasts doing more holding than straight compression.

The bra is featherlight and breathable but be forewarned, there’s a lot of cup to these cups. I get that it’s an aesthetics thing, but it is wild seeing yourself in a sports bra that adds to your breasts. If you’re not opposed to more boobs than ever on a run (and honestly, it looked good to me!), and you want a simple, affordable bra, this is a great option.

In a recent development, this extremely reasonably priced back-pocket bra is one of my top picks from my sports bras with pocket testing. The phone pocket is easy to reach, and, unlike other pocket bras, there isn’t an overload of material along the back strap design. That does mean the pocket is shallower than similar models, and I find myself reaching back to make sure my phone is still there (I haven’t lost it yet, but it’s something to keep in mind).

Sources indicate that this bra is available in a ridiculous array of fun colors, has an easy-to-wear shape, and features a well-fitted design with good coverage and comfort for most cup sizes. For those of us wearing wired headphones, you can thread the cords through a bonded eyelet above the pocket, and the bra stays quite odor resistant even after sweaty workout sessions.

To determine your sports bra size, Lawson uses this system of measuring:.

According to recent reports, but this equation isn’t doctrine. There is no industry standard for bra sizing; not every brand follows the same conventions of measurement. Some brands, for instance, instruct customers to add 4 or 5 inches to the band measurement to determine band size.

“I’ve been creating, evaluating, revising, critiquing sports bra fit charts for decades for brands large and small,” Lawson says. “Because our bodies and breasts are so diverse, it’s virtually impossible for any brand to create the perfect sizing scheme and fit chart that works for 100 percent of women.” But Lawson calls this “a blessing,” comparing sports bras to jeans. Imagine if every size 10 jean had a standardized fit. That would alienate curvier, thinner, shorter, or taller individuals. “It can take trial and error to find your perfect jeans fit match, but once you do it can be a life-changer.” And the same goes for sports bras.

She offers some tips to navigate the Wild West of bra sizing.

When it comes to support, there are two basic sports bra designs: compression and encapsulation. Compression is when strong elastic materials are used to compress your chest. Encapsulation is when each breast is supported separately in its own cup. According to Lawson, many women with larger breasts prefer encapsulation because they find it more comfortable. “It’s not smooshing everything together, trapping moisture between the breasts,” she indicates. That being mentioned, some encapsulation bras, such as the SheFit, Janji, and lululemon Run Times, also offer degrees of compression inside the encapsulation, which serve as both impact protection and an additional layer of support and protection for larger-busted people or those who have lost volume.

In a recent development, regardless of the type of chest design, an adjustable waistband and shoulder straps help improve overall support when you have larger breasts. More padded straps won’t necessarily translate to a more comfortable fit, Lawson notes. Putting in more foam may initially feel more comfortable, but it won’t decrease pressure. “The one thing that will decrease strap pressure is a wider strap. If you make the strap twice as wide, it doesn’t quite cut the shoulder pressure in half, but it’ll take it almost down to half.”.

Recent findings suggest that some of my favorite racing shorts are pocketless, which isn’t a major deal—when your sports bra has pockets. Some brands offer bras with side pockets and front pockets for housing keys or gels. There are bras with back pockets for storing your smartphone as well. A thing to note with bra storage is that you could be sacrificing support if you weigh down your bra with items.

Some people believe that storing your phone in your bra can increase your breast cancer risk. “There is no conclusive data to suggest that cell phones are linked to cancer,” claims Diana Medgyesy, MD, a medical oncologist at UCHealth. However, she adds that “this is an evolving field since cell phone technology and the use of cell phones are changing rapidly,” so use your own discretion on whether or not to run with your phone in your bra.

In a recent development, when it comes to finding the best sports bra for you, patience and some trial and error are key. “Be prepared to become a sleuth,” Lawson says. “Be prepared to do a little work to understand your own body/breasts and then a lot of work to sleuth out brands whose fit philosophies and metrics match your needs and preferences.

“Most of us are willing to try a dozen or more running shoe brands/styles/sizes to get the best product match for our feet and workouts—give your sports bra quest the same effort and attention to detail.”.

In a recent development, one population of runners we don’t want to leave out is those who have had lumpectomies, mastectomies, or other breast surgeries. That’s why we spoke with breast surgeon and runner Deborah M. Capko, MD, FACS, from Memorial Sloan Kettering in Upcoming York City. She says that “it’s all about compression” for women who have had breast surgery. For up to a year after surgery, you could be dealing with swelling and discomfort during your runs. Having a compressive bra like a SheFit or lululemon Run Times bra can help.

In a recent development, capko states underwires are a no-go, but keeping your post-op breasts “stable and highly supported” can cut down on that swelling and pain. We also spoke with a few runners who have run postmastectomy and lumpectomy, and they agree. When it comes to preferred bra design, they suggested clasp or zip over pullover because a pullover is harder to deal with and far less comfortable.

What is the best sports bra type for running?

Ideally, you want a bra that has a medium or high level of support, a secure, but not too tight band, and straps that sit just before the acromion bone (the boney protuberance at the top of your shoulder.

What Makes a Sports Bra High Impact?

It has been revealed that high-impact sports bras are made to decrease breast movement while you’re performing high-impact activities. They usually use some sort of compression, encapsulated cups, molded cups, supportive fabrics, wider bands, and adjustable straps or closures or combination of these to create a secure fit.

According to recent reports, A running sports bra should feel supportive and pretty darn snug without making you feel like you can’t breathe. The band should sit nicely around your torso, under your breasts, and the cups should fully contain your breasts. The straps shouldn’t slip, and if you’re noticing slipping of any area during your run, it either needs adjustment or you need a new size.

Getting a bra with flat-locked seams like those on this list, with well-fitting straps and the correct cup size is the most vital thing. Having good, moisture-wicking fabric allows it to dry faster to prevent friction. Before you head out on a long run, do a shorter workout first to try to notice potential hot spots.

How Often Should You Wash Your Sports Bra?

It has been revealed that you can wear your bra several times before washing, but be sure to wash it at least every couple of runs. Because you’re sweating in the sports bra during running, which is a high-intensity activity, your bra can develop bacteria buildup (gross).

Industry observers note that most sports bras can be tossed into the washing machine, but read the garment label just in case. Refrain from adding in fabric softener, since that can degrade the material and interfere with its breathability and moisture-wicking properties.

Air-drying is strongly recommended, although you can put the bra in the dryer on a tumble setting. Heat from your machine can degrade the bra’s structure as well.

How long does a sports bra last?

Like a running shoe, sports bra shelf life is dependent on the wearer. While it’s recommended you retire your sports bra once or twice a year, we get it—you’ve formed an attachment. But there are telltale signs that it’s time to say goodbye. If the straps are overstretched, the band is loose or causes friction when it never used to, the cups have lost shape, or there’s a hole in the fabric, time for a new bra.

According to recent reports, another sign to go shopping: your body has changed and the bra doesn’t fit like it used to. It’s worth buying a upcoming sports bra that gives you proper support instead of willing an old bra to give you support it can no longer provide.

Bra manufacturers have a real matter creating a full range of sizes for high-impact sports bras. It is rare to find a bra that goes above a 42DDD. SheFit manages, and a few select other brands, but in general, bras with band sizes above 42 and cup sizes above DDD are hard to come by. This is an error in the industry that makes it difficult for people in larger bodies to achieve their running and fitness goals comfortably. Plus-size runners are wildly underrepresented across the span of gear. Running and running gear should be accessible for all, no matter the size of body you live in.

Runner’s World began covering all things running in 1966, but the first sports bra, the Jogbra, wasn’t invented until a decade later. Sports bras are as necessary as a pair of running shoes. Since their invention, they continue to undergo changes in design and tech.

Sources indicate that we researched the history of the sports bra and combed through the products available on the market today. We spoke with designers, brand representatives, and experts in the field, including LaJean Lawson, PhD.

Known as Dr. Sports Bra in her field, Lawson has two graduate degrees in sports bra science and is the principal at Creative Fitness Solutions in Portland, Oregon.

The collegiate fall racing calendar isn't quite finished, with the 2026 NCAA Cross Country National Championships bringing together teams and individual athletes looking to end their seasons with a title.

Industry observers note that division I gets underway Saturday, November 21, in Terre Haute, Indiana, where 32 men's teams and 32 women's teams will compete. Alongside them will be 38 individual qualifiers whose schools didn't make the team field.

Sources indicate that if you've been keeping a close eye on college cross country this season, there's plenty to be excited about this weekend. Oklahoma State returns as the defending men's team champion and winners of two of the past three titles, while NC State's women will look to add another trophy to a particularly successful stretch of their own, having collected four championships since 2021.

In a recent development, fortunately, you don't have to make the trip to Indiana to catch the action. Here's when everything starts, where the races are being held, and how to watch from home.

The Division I and Division III championships will both take place on Saturday, November 21, although the two competitions will be held in different states.

Division II runners will have to wait a little longer, with their national championship scheduled for Friday, December 4.

According to the NCAA's championship schedule, here's where each division will compete:.

For Division I, ESPNU and the ESPN app will carry the national championships live on Saturday, November 21, with coverage beginning at 10 a.m. ET.

The women's 6K starts at 10:20 a.m., followed by the men's 10K at 11:10 a.m., and the trophy presentation scheduled for around noon.

Fans following Divisions II and III can watch their respective competitions through the NCAA.com's live streaming schedule.

Oklahoma State has been tough to beat in recent years, finishing near the top of the men’s standings more often than not. The Cowboys have claimed two of the last five national titles, winning the national title in 2025, with 57 points, 25 points ahead of runner-up New Mexico.

NC State’s women have enjoyed a similarly strong run, having won three straight titles from 2021 to 2023, before BYU took the 2024 championship. NC State reclaimed the top spot last year, with 114 points.

Division I's national field includes 32 teams per gender, with 18 earning automatic spots through the nine regional championships and another 14 receiving bids through an at-large selection process.

In a recent development, there are also 38 individual qualifiers in each race, representing schools that didn't advance as teams, so the competition for the individual titles extends well beyond the athletes wearing jerseys from the leading programs. With both individual and team titles on the line, there's plenty to follow once the starting gun goes off.

The Bivo Trio Mini Keeps Finding a Place on Our Bikes When the Temperatures Begin to Dip—Here’s Why

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • In a recent development, your water bottles have probably frozen at least once if you ride outside in cold weather.
  • There are proven ways to keep your bottles from freezing—or carry hot beverages on rides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

In a recent development, your water bottles have probably frozen at least once if you ride outside in cold weather. Usually, it’s only a thin layer of ice on top or a clogged nozzle, but that’s enough to be annoying. If you ride at low enough temperatures with standard plastic bottles filled with plain water, it will inevitably happen. However, it’s important to stay hydrated on winter rides.

There are proven ways to keep your bottles from freezing—or carry hot beverages on rides. Hot chocolate, coffee, tea, or Skratch Labs’ apple cider will warm your soul and lift your mood. And nothing hits better than a coffee stop in the middle of a cold winter ride, especially when conditions are dreary or sloppy.

Stainless insulated bottles broke into cycling about five years ago and have since exploded in popularity. They’re a proven way to keep water and hydration mix cool on the hottest summer days, and they can also keep hot drinks warm for many miles on winter rides.

Recent findings suggest that the Bivo Trio Bottle, available in raw stainless steel and silicone-covered stainless steel versions, has become a bottle of choice on cold-weather rides. Read on to find out why, plus tips to prevent your bottles from freezing this winter.

FULL COLD WEATHER BOTTLE TEST RESULTS.

Cyclists have many different methods (often handed down from one generation of riders to the next) to help prevent frozen bottles. One simple solution is to start your ride with hot water. However, depending on the temperature and ride length, this can also freeze.

Sources indicate that using insulated plastic bottles, adding a high-sodium drink mix, and wearing a hydration pack or vest under a riding jacket are all tricks I’ve used (with varying degrees of success) to keep my bottles from freezing. And some riders still swear by adding a shot of booze to their bidon. However, while these methods may prevent icing, they still result in a cold beverage during your ride.

In a recent development, it’s hard to miss the growing popularity of stainless steel water bottles in cycling. Their use has boomed in the last few seasons as more riders have become concerned about microplastic contamination. Plus, these metal bidons, particularly the Bivo bottles, are in the cages of many cycling influencers.

Recent findings suggest that stainless bottles typically feature a vacuum-sealed double-wall design with a coated outer and a bare stainless inner layer. Since metal bottles are rigid, you cannot squeeze them like plastic bottles. (It takes some getting used to if you haven’t ridden them before.) And while stainless bottles are much heavier than plastic models, they are heavy-duty and almost indestructible—they dent and scratch but rarely break.

Bivo is the trend-setting stainless option and commonly available from retailers like REI, Backcountry, Amazon, or your local bike shop. The Insulated Mini we tested is 17 ounces and costs $44, or opt for the 21-ounce model for $5 more.

Recent findings suggest that I have ridden with insulated bottles at several points in my cycling life. But until last summer, I usually stuck with non-insulated plastic bottles for most of my rides, regardless of air temperature.

It has been revealed that generally, I prefer the feel of a regular bottle; 22-ounce Specialized Purist bottles are my go-to, and I occasionally carry a 10-ounce Purist Maker mug for a mid-ride coffee break. But I often skip stainless insulated bottles because they aren’t squeezable and weigh noticeably more than plastic bidons.

However, before a recent ride on a cold and blustery day, I filled an insulated bottle with hot chocolate and was pleased to have a warm treat throughout my 90-minute ride. So, like my insulated bottle test last summer, I applied a little science to see which insulated stainless bottles performed best in cold temps.

According to recent reports, for this test, I gathered several popular metal insulated bottles. First, I evaluated the bottles by measuring water temperature over three hours in subfreezing conditions. Then, I used them on rides in cold weather to determine which worked best from a functional perspective.

While the intent was somewhat scientific, I also strove to be practical—these are tests anyone can do at home. This testing was not performed in a controlled environment or with professional-level, calibrated equipment.

In a recent development, since it was below 32 degrees outside, I was able to perform outdoor freeze testing. Like my summer insulated bottle tests, I filled the selected bottles with 400 grams of tap water (heated to 212 degrees for this test instead of chilled water used in summer). Then I placed the filled bottles on my front porch in subfreezing temperatures; I did this after sunset so sunlight would not warm the bottles. Every 30 minutes, I checked and recorded the water temperature of each bottle, in the same order each time, with a digital food thermometer.

Following the initial three-hour test period, the bottles remained overnight in sub-freezing temperatures for an additional nine hours. This tested whether the contents would stay warm for a full 12 hours (as per some bottle makers’ claims). Additionally, for reference, I subjected a Purist Maker tumbler (with 200 grams of water), an insulated plastic bottle, and a standard plastic bottle to the same tests.

The following day, I evaluated the bottles’ on-bike performance on a short loop in my neighborhood. I tested their use with standard and lobster-claw gloves (such as holding, opening caps, removing them from cages) and their nozzles’ function while drinking hot coffee (a medium-roast pour-over with some oat milk for my tests 😉).

In a recent development, the results were clear: Insulated stainless bottles work very well in cold weather. They keep your beverage hot for an hour-long ride in 30-degree temps. For longer rides, your drink will experience some heat loss but will remain drinkably warm for three hours. The insulated metal bottles performed notably better than plastic bottles (insulated and non-insulated) for the full duration of the test.

Recent findings suggest that after about three hours of exposure in the cold, the Bivo Insulated Trio Mini kept my coffee at a warm 119.8 degrees. This is only slightly below coffee expert James Hoffmann’s recommended coffee-drinking temp of 122 to 129 degrees. (Although I’m not sure Hoffmann would be pleased drinking three-hour-old brew.) In 12-hour testing, none of the metal bottles froze. Most bottles finished at room temperature after 12 hours outside in freezing temperatures.

Recent findings suggest that on the bike, the Bivo valve works great, and the bottle texture isn’t overly slippery. The bottle shape is compatible with most cages, though it fits best in the Arundle Sport cage recommended by Bivo.

Nozzle Shield: Look for bottles with a cap that protects the nozzle. Typically, I’m not a fan of these shields when riding in warm weather—they flop around and get in the way when drinking. However, in the winter, caps keep road salt and slush off the bottle’s nozzle, and they also help prevent icing. Ones with a removable plastic or rubber shield are easier to clean; plus, you can use the bottles without the cap on warm days.

According to recent reports, vapor Pressure: Many of the tested bottles carry a warning about using liquids hotter than 180 degrees. This is to avoid scalding and burns from pressurized hot water when the cap or nozzle is opened. With insulated bottles, hot liquid heats the air inside the bottle enough to spray potentially near-boiling water into your mouth or onto your body.

Avoid this by letting your hot beverage cool slightly before pouring it into your bottle. For long rides (when using two bottles of hot drinks), save the hotter bottle for later in the day. This way, it has time to cool to a drinkable temperature.

Cage Compatibility: Since they do not deform or flex, metal bottles don’t pair with every bottle cage. Some stainless bottles have a loose fit in cages (bottles can even eject on rough roads), and some cage shapes do not allow some metal bottles to sit correctly, causing annoying rattling and buzzing while riding. Other cage-bottle pairings are so tight that it’s hard to remove the bottle while riding.

In a recent development, my advice: Check that your cages work before dropping up to $100 for new bottles that won’t fit. Some brands have specific cage recommendations on their sites. You can also read user reviews for the compatibility of different bottles and cages. Also, be sure to check the overall bottle height to be sure it fits in your frame.

Dropped Bottles: I do not recommend using metal bottles in mass-start situations; use plastic bidons for substantial group rides or races. When a metal bottle is ejected from a cage on a bump, or you drop one (as is prone to happen with cold hands or when wearing bulky gloves), it ricochets off the road surface more than a plastic bottle. And while metal makes these bottles more durable, they do not burst open on impact or crush if hit by other riders.

Bivo shook up the bottle market when it launched its stainless steel bottles. The small Richmond, Vermont-based company launched insulated bottles shortly after, and cyclists have fallen in love with them. They work well, look good, and don’t have a funky taste.

In a recent development, as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that emma Grace Hurley, Weini Kelati, and Jess McClain already had plenty to celebrate after earning the United States its first women's team medal at September's World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen. But nearly two months after finishing with silver, the American trio could soon have gold added to their résumés.

In a recent development, on Thursday, November 19, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) declared that Kenya's Veronica Loleo had received a three-year doping ban after testing positive for erythropoietin (EPO), a prohibited substance. The decision officially disqualifies her second-place finish at the September 20 event, where her silver medal helped Kenya secure the women's team title. But with Loleo's result now thrown out, Kenya's team score has to be recalculated. Countries are ranked by the combined finishing times of their three fastest athletes, and Loleo’s removal means Kenya must now count Lilian Kasait Rengeruk, who finished 34th in 1:10:36, potentially lifting the U.S. to first place in the team standings.

The Kenyan women originally led with a combined 3:17:33, ahead of the Americans' 3:19:51. But removing Loleo's 1:06:05 pushes Kenya's total to 3:22:04, leaving the U.S. in first place by two minutes and 13 seconds. Kenya would drop to second and Ethiopia would remain third, although World Athletics has yet to officially confirm the updated results.

It has been revealed that hurley recently acknowledged the uncertainty in a comment on Citius Mag's Instagram, noting that nobody can know exactly how the race would've unfolded without Loleo. Still, she admitted, "it would've been so cool to celebrate gold 🥹.".

Industry observers note that loleo's sample was collected during an out-of-competition test on September 6 ahead of the championships, two weeks prior to the competition. She initially told investigators she couldn't explain the positive result, mentioning an injection she'd received for an injury, but later admitted to the violation on October 30, which earned her a one-year reduction from the standard four-year suspension.

According to recent reports, loleo wasn't the only major Kenyan distance runner to receive a final decision Thursday. Peres Jepchirchir, the reigning world marathon champion and 2021 Olympic gold medalist, was also handed a three-year ban following an EPO finding.

“The Kenyan authorities have made a lot of progress in the fight against doping in the last five years, but these cases highlight that there is still a long way to go,” AIU chief executive Brett Clothier said in a statement.

“The Kenyan government is aware of the current situation and has committed to further strengthen the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya and take action to address the criminal networks that facilitate doping within the country.”.

Recent findings suggest that jepchirchir, who had been provisionally suspended in October, has accepted the disqualification of her results dating back to July 17, including her August victory at the Sydney Marathon. Fellow Kenyan Irine Cheptai is expected to inherit that title.

The Anti-Movement Core Routine Every Runner Needs

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: Aleksandr Kondratov, Getty).
  • It has been revealed that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a upcoming study on anti-movement vs.
  • In a recent development, “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Glute bridge post-run. (Photo: Aleksandr Kondratov, Getty).

It has been revealed that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a upcoming study on anti-movement vs. dynamic core training and built a simple, science-backed core routine for runners based on the findings. The routine targets the deep stabilizing muscles that protect your spine and improve performance.

In a recent development, “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around. We all know we need it. But what exactly is it, and what should it entail? (Hint: Not crunches.).

When we talk about the core, we mean the abdominal muscles, low back, gluteal, pelvic, and hip muscles that support the spine and trunk. These muscles include both smaller, deep groups that attach directly to the spine to provide stabilization and larger, more global ones that can assist with stability and produce movement.

Sources indicate that why do we need this area to be strong? Well, even non-runners need to pay attention to their core strength to avoid lower back pain, which is the top cause of years lived with disability. Athletically, the core must create proximal stability to allow for powerful, efficient movements distally—which requires adequate strength combined with coordinated neuromuscular activation and control. So, core strength is certainly important for pain reduction, injury prevention, and athletic performance.

Sources indicate that when running, the trunk serves to provide a stable base of support so that the legs can effectively generate the forces that create forward movement. These forces are transferred across the trunk and counterbalanced by the arms, requiring coordination between the hips, trunk muscles, and shoulders.

Recent findings suggest that while running appears to be purely a forward (sagittal plane) activity, the trunk muscles are hard at work controlling side-to-side (frontal plane) and rotational (transverse plane) forces. Muscle activation and timing change with speed, with higher speeds generally requiring more control and work. The deep trunk muscles also contribute to respiration.

It has been revealed that while some small trunk motion naturally occurs with running, excessive motion is detrimental. Increased trunk flexion is associated with decreased running economy and increased loading rates and vertical impact forces. Increased lateral trunk lean has also been linked to increased loading rates, which may play a role in the development of certain injuries.

Even though most of us know that crunches are out, there’s still plenty of confusion about how to train our cores. While strength work doesn’t need to look exactly like running, it does need to meet (and exceed) its demands—meaning that stability should be emphasized over motion.

Enter a recent study comparing neuromuscular activation between “anti-movement” and “dynamic” core training. Unlike traditional dynamic core exercises, which work the trunk and spinal musculature by moving through flexion, extension, rotation, and side bending, anti-movement exercises resist external forces, forcing stabilization throughout the trunk—basically, trunk isometrics.

The 12-week study compared a combination of Pallof holds and plank variations (incorporating bands and the TRX suspension trainer for progression) in the anti-movement program against a dynamic program that included exercises such as sit-ups, leg raises, jack knives, Russian twists, windshield wipers, and back extensions (incorporating Swiss balls for progression).

While both exercise groups demonstrated enhancements in neuromuscular efficiency compared to a control group, improvements were overall greater in the anti-movement group, particularly within the deep local musculature that activates prior to limb movement and plays an important role in stabilizing the spine.

The authors therefore hypothesized that this enhanced neuromuscular efficiency could improve endurance, delay fatigue, and reduce the need for recruitment of larger, more global muscles—thus protecting the spine and potentially decreasing injury risk while improving performance.

Runners can apply these findings and consider an “anti-movement”-focused core routine, similar to the one used in the study. Nothing fancy or extensive is required—just one exercise each to resist the trunk’s motions (flexion, extension, rotation, and side-bending/lateral flexion). Simple plank variations and other holds work well to streamline your core routine efficiently and effectively.

Targets: Anti-extension · full core (local and global).

The front plank is a classic core stability exercise that falls into the anti-extension category, challenging most of both the local and global core muscles.

Targets: Anti-flexion · spinal extensors and glutes.

While the study used a supine plank as its anti-flexion exercise, the shoulder position required could be a limiter, so bridge holds are likely a more practical way for many runners to work the posterior trunk muscles, including the spinal extensors and gluteals.

Targets: Anti-lateral flexion · lateral trunk and hip muscles.

The side plank can be considered an anti-lateral-flexion exercise, challenging the lateral trunk and hip musculature.

Targets: Anti-rotation · obliques and deep abdominal rotators.

The Pallof press is a common anti-rotation exercise, challenging the deep abdominal rotators, including the obliques.

Sources indicate that sit cross-legged or in another comfortable position. Reach your arms toward the sky. Exhale as you lean toward the left, keeping your arms overhead, and feeling a stretch along your right side. Inhale and return to center with your arms overhead. Exhale as you bend toward the right, feeling a stretch along your left side. Inhale and return to center.

In a recent development, from your seated position, reach your arms out to the sides in a T shape. Inhale as you reach your chest forward, lift your gaze toward the sky, bend your elbows, and draw your arms slightly behind you in seated Cow Pose. Exhale as you draw your navel toward your spine, round your back, and wrap your arms around yourself in a seated Cat Pose variation. Repeat a few times at your own pace.

It has been revealed that reach your arms straight out to the sides. Exhale as you turn your palms toward the sky and your elbows to face the floor. Reach your thumbs toward the wall behind you and your pinkies toward the sky. Take a few breaths here.

Exhale as you rotate your arms forward almost 360 degrees so your elbows and palms face the sky again. Reach your thumbs toward the wall behind you and your pinkies forward. Take a few breaths here.

Industry observers note that exhale and twist your chest toward the right. Place your left hand on your right knee and your right fingertips on the mat behind you. Take a few breaths here.

Recent findings suggest that inhale and return to center. Reach both arms overhead, then twist your chest toward the left. Place your right hand on your left knee and your left fingertips on the mat behind you. Take a few breaths here, then return to center.

According to recent reports, sit with your legs bent, feet on the mat, and your hands behind your hips with your fingertips pointing toward your body. Exhale and press your hands and feet into the mat as you lift your hips into Reverse Tabletop. Gaze forward or at the sky. Breathe here. As you exhale, lower your hips back to the mat.

Lower your right toes to the mat, then the left.

Recent findings suggest that sit on the mat and draw the soles of your feet together, as close or as far from your hips as feels comfortable. Inhale and lift your chest. Stay here for a few breaths or you can instead make it a dynamic stretch if you lean forward, roll to an upright position, and then reach your chest forward over your legs again, repeating that motion a few times. From your hands and knees, tuck your toes, sink your hips toward your heels, and walk your hands back until you’re sitting on your heels in Toe Squat. If the stretch along the bottoms of your feet is too intense, you can keep your hands on the mat and your chest leaning forward to help minimize the stretch. Take a few breaths here.

Return to your hands and knees.

Lower your knees, chest, and chin to the mat. Press your hands and the tops of your feet into the mat as you lift your chest any amount in Cobra Pose.

Return to your hands and knees. Tuck your toes and shift your hips up and back into Downward-Facing Dog. Take a few deep breaths here.

#217423. How Beginners Can Build Cycling Endurance in Just 3 Days a Week

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2028 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

How Beginners Can Build Cycling Endurance in Just 3 Days a Week

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building a base on the bike has traditionally meant putting in a lot of hours doing long, slow distance training.
  • In a recent development, as it turns out, especially if you’re a newer cyclist, there’s a lot that you can accomplish if you only have three days a week to get on the bike.
  • Here, we spoke with Namrita Brooke, Ph.D., one of the lead coaches at BaseCamp, about how she would structure the optimal three-day week on the bike—and what other lifestyle tweaks she would make in order to improve fitness even when you can’t fit in long rides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building a base on the bike has traditionally meant putting in a lot of hours doing long, slow distance training. But with work and family lives, it can feel impossible to find the hours in the week to properly commit to a base build, especially if you’re a beginner cyclist who’s not used to rides that take more than three hours.

In a recent development, as it turns out, especially if you’re a newer cyclist, there’s a lot that you can accomplish if you only have three days a week to get on the bike. Building a base of fitness for cycling takes some commitment and consistency, but it doesn’t have to take over your life.

Here, we spoke with Namrita Brooke, Ph.D., one of the lead coaches at BaseCamp, about how she would structure the optimal three-day week on the bike—and what other lifestyle tweaks she would make in order to improve fitness even when you can’t fit in long rides.

In a recent development, A lot of cyclists think that if they can’t train 10-plus hours per week, their fitness will suffer, or they won’t make gains on the bike. This isn’t true, especially for newer riders. “Someone who has not been doing any exercise would see gains in as little as two to four hours a week of riding,” indicates Brooke. “If someone has some general fitness, gains could be had in four to six hours [per week].”.

However, expect that after a few weeks or months, the tangible signs of progress will slow unless you can devote more time to training. “The tricky part is the ongoing gains might not be as easy to see as the initial gains,” Brooke adds. “Initially, if the athlete was measuring power, they would see power increases, but these would plateau in a few months, leading them to think gains are no longer occurring but in reality, the athlete is likely to still build other metrics of fitness like repeatability, durability, and resilience, but those are not as easy to measure.”.

In a recent development, often, new cyclists with limited time tend to attempt one monster ride on the weekend, skipping cycling during the week due to busy lives. But even if you can only eke out two one-hour (or 45-minute!) trainer sessions on weekdays in addition to the long weekend ride, you’ll gain fitness and strength faster than if you stick to a single ride.

“I would rather see the athlete do three quality days a week versus one or even two longer days,” claims Brooke.

“The base training goal, whether you’re a pro or average Joe, is to build the best aerobic fitness you can for the training hours you have available,” indicates Brooke. Without this aerobic fitness, you won’t be able to boost your speed or power on the bike.

This means spending the bulk of your time on the bike in zone 2 (whether you use power, heart rate or perceived exertion). Riding in zone 2—also known as your endurance pace—will mean that you’re able to hold a conversation and speak in full sentences, but it should feel slightly difficult to do so. If you can chat away easily, you’re riding a little too easy. If you’re gasping for air between sentences, you’re riding a little too hard.

According to recent reports, by that, we mean your skin. Riding more miles means being aware of skin considerations such as sun protection and chafing prevention. Don’t just ignore reddened skin, use lubricants and padded shorts to feel more comfortable on the bike.

For newer riders, opt for the longer durations in each phase. If you’ve been riding for a while, you’ll likely notice that after a few weeks in each phase, you’re at a point where you’re not noticing any improvements—in that case, proceed to the next phase. Here’s how Brooke would break it down.

2.5-3.5 hours (zone 2), based on how much free time you have available.

Newly introduced riders may need to break up the zone 3 portion of the ride with an easy 5-10 minutes in the middle.

2.5-4 hour (zone 2) based on how much free time you have available.

Sources indicate that have an extra hour on Saturday for your long ride? Great! Woke up an hour early on Wednesday and have time to hop on the trainer for an extra 45-minute ride in zone 2? Fantastic. Feel free to add time whenever possible.

In a recent development, four days on the bike is better than three, says Brooke. “Two harder interval days and two longer days would be best if possible,” she notes. And this is actually a fairly standard schedule for most serious cyclists—they’ll add one or two additional easy rides to the schedule, but the meat and potatoes of their training consists of two longer endurance rides and two harder interval-based sessions.

In fact, Brooke indicates that often, she hears new cyclists say they only have four hours per week to train, but once they get going, they start to “find” extra time. “You would be surprised how many newer riders think they are limited to four to six hours a week but once they really get into cycling, they make accommodations to squeeze in an extra hour or two per week,” she says. “I see riders all the time start to wake up earlier to squeeze in additional ride time before they start the rest of the day!”.

It has been revealed that and thanks to the prevalence of indoor trainers, it’s easier than ever to sneak in an extra hour or two on the bike during a weekend or early in the morning, even if you have work or childcare demands on your time. But don’t neglect outdoor riding, especially if your base-building goal is to be able to keep up on the local group ride or jump into a race. While indoor training builds fitness, it doesn’t help improve your skills for riding outdoors, so make time for at least one outdoor ride per week if at all possible.

Sources indicate that there is one final caveat: It’s easy to get excited about the prospect of adding a monster ride to your weekend whenever possible, but these long rides aren’t easy. Four hours on the bike will feel very, very different from two hours. If riding for five hours on Saturday means you can barely walk for two days after, or it impacts your training the next week, back off.

Sources indicate that long rides shouldn’t leave you flattened for days afterwards. If they do, you’re doing too much, too soon. And Brooke notes that the longer you ride, the more important it is to properly fuel that long effort!

The fastest way to improve your fitness is—again—by consistently training. But training doesn’t mean all-bike-all-the-time! Brooke states there are quite a few simple additions you can do on those non-cycling days to see gains on the bike.

According to recent reports, → Walk: Often on conference calls for work, or accompanying your kiddos to soccer practice? Walk and talk, or do laps around the field while you cheer. “Walking is more of an aerobic builder than people think and can be a gentle form of aerobic activity to accompany bike time,” Brooke claims.

For the office worker, treadmill desks are becoming more popular, and if you do want to put in more bike time and you have a stationary trainer, you can do some easy spinning while answering emails or brainstorming for that massive presentation.

Sources indicate that → Strength Train: “Strength training can be added in as little as 15 minutes a day, three days a week if we are willing to change the paradigm of going to the gym and lifting heavy things,” says Brooke. “Integrating just this small amount of functional strength into a base training program like we do at BaseCamp yields long-term benefits to your training and health.”.

You can do shortstrength sessions at home with just a couple of weights, or even bodyweight alone to get started.

Recent findings suggest that in a typical training proposal, cyclists have three weeks of training followed by a rest week where they do only a couple of shorter, easier rides. When you’re only able to ride three days a week, there’s no reason to take a rest week—you’re already getting plenty of recovery time in the four days you’re off the bike.

Recent findings suggest that “The low training stimulus is likely not enough to elicit a high enough super-compensation response to make the loss of fitness during a rest week worth it,” indicates Brooke. (That said, if you’re a beginner rider and find that after three weeks, you are feeling fatigued, you can dial down the duration or intensity for that fourth week—but stick to three rides if possible.).

Industry observers note that once you’ve done your base training for several weeks with your rides spread out through the week (i.e Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday), you may want to try switching things up. If you do have the ability to try out new riding days, it’s worth experimenting with doing mini-training blocks, i.e riding three days in a row, some weeks. This subtle shift changes your training stimulus by forcing your body to contend with the need for speedier recovery between rides.

In a recent development, newer riders may find that it’s harder to recover between rides in these chunks, claims Brooke. “The challenge of block training is the athlete needs a certain amount of base fitness to be able to respond and adapt to this type of stimuli and in this scenario,” she explains. “But testing the block process is the only way to find out how they tolerate it.”.

If you try riding three days in a row and feel exhausted, go back to your regular schedule and test again after another few weeks of consistent training.

According to recent reports, while it’s tempting to stay in the base phase forever, this training phase should really only last around eight weeks. At this point, your aerobic fitness is maximized (for now) and it’s time to focus on the development of “power.”.

According to recent reports, “After the base phase comes the build phase, where the athlete wants to increase their sustainable max power for a range of times,” says Brooke. “For a newer cyclist without a specific goal, focus on holding a higher wattage for five minutes to 40 minutes. This phase should be maintained as long as the athlete continues to see improvement, then once response begins to fade, move on to the next phases.”.

Once you’ve plateaued your power gains, the final phase, typically utilized when “peaking” for an event would be the “speed” phase, explains Brooke. “Here, the cyclist would focus on improving shorter efforts of under five minutes and building anaerobic capacity to focus on performing better in events or group rides.”.

After your main event, whether it’s a race or group ride or even just spending four to six weeks focusing on upping your sprint power, it’s time to take a short break and then circle back to base phase.

The good news is that once you’ve completed this cycle, you’ll be pleasantly surprised at how much stronger you’re feeling on the bike the second time you tackle base training. While training phases are cyclical, your fitness grows as you spend more and more time on the bike, so no training phase will feel exactly the same.

#217422. This Mileage Target Can Help You Determine Whether You Built a Strong Enough Base to Start Race Training

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (724 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

This Mileage Target Can Help You Determine Whether You Built a Strong Enough Base to Start Race Training

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that base training involves spending a few weeks running at an easy pace and slowly increasing your mileage over time.
  • In a recent development, building a sufficient aerobic base helps you avoid the aches and pains that come with ramping up mileage too swiftly, especially if you’ve been running sporadically or took some time off.
  • The hard part of this foundational phase?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that base training involves spending a few weeks running at an easy pace and slowly increasing your mileage over time. It’s a crucial first step in any running journey, designed to help you ease into race-specific training.

In a recent development, building a sufficient aerobic base helps you avoid the aches and pains that come with ramping up mileage too swiftly, especially if you’ve been running sporadically or took some time off. It also makes running feel more doable, as it bridges the gap between your current routine and your goal training initiative.

The hard part of this foundational phase? Figuring out if you’re ready to tackle the first few weeks of a blueprint and start race-specific workouts. Thankfully, coaches offer a helpful benchmark to hit, plus they explain how to smoothly transition your base routine to race training, without shocking your system.

Building a strong base before racing any distance helps prevent injuries and improves long-term performance, including improved aerobic capacity, endurance, faster recovery, mental conditioning, and weight and stress management, Jill Becker, a personal trainer and run coach at Life Time in Westminster, CO, previously told Runner’s World. That’s why the phase is necessary for all runners, whether you’re new to the sport or have a Boston qualifying time on the list of goals.

“Even a 5K race relies heavily on aerobic systems for energy production—so the better the aerobic base you have, the faster you can race,” Laura Norris, owner and coach at Laura Norris Running in Boulder, CO, previously told Runner’s World.

Additionally, Norris says doing these easy miles weeks before your goal training block allows your body to adapt to the mileage first, so you can then add in speedwork leading up to race day with lower risk of injury and burnout. Taking this approach helps you avoid increasing volume and intensity at the same time, which can often lead to overtraining.

Finally, tackling a base phase means you’ll feel more confident heading into, say, a four-miler with faster-paced efforts (like tempo or race pace miles), as you’ll have already run four miles at an easy pace consistently for several weeks.

Building a strong base requires covering a certain number of miles consistently over the course of several weeks. Beginners should aim to spend at least 10 weeks on this training block, while intermediate runners can follow a six-week proposal, and more advanced runners typically need about four weeks to set that aerobic foundation, Becker notes.

It has been revealed that if you’ve already picked out your training initiative, Norris recommends working up to at least 80 percent of the weekly mileage prescribed in the first week of that plan. For example, our 20-week beginner marathon plan prescribes 12 miles in the first week. That means you’ll want to work up to about 10 miles per week before diving into the plan. If you’re looking to break two hours in the half marathon, which requires running at least 18 miles in the first week of the Runner’s World plan, then you’ll want to work up to about 15 miles.

If you haven’t identified your training blueprint yet, Becker recommends adding at least 10 miles to your current weekly volume. (If you’re right now running 10 miles a week, work up to 20.).

Look for a proposal that builds up to that mileage goal slowly, following the 10 percent rule, which means increasing your mileage by no more than 10 percent each week.

Keep in mind, base training is about setting the foundation for your next training block, and a part of that process should include recovery time. This means making time for rest days and down weeks (in which you reduce your volume to allow for recovery and better performance), as well as staying on top of your nutrition, sleep habits, and cross-training.

Best Winter Cycling Gloves for Cold, Wet, and Windy Rides
