If you don’t like the taste of creatine powder or find it a pain to mix, Optimum Nutrition Micronized Creatine Capsules are a convenient and tasteless alternative. Plus, a bottle of these capsules will take up less room in your gym bag than a tub of creatine powder.

Optimum Nutrition offers three sizes: 100 capsules for $30 ($0.60/serving), 200 capsules for $50 ($0.50/serving), or 300 capsules for $69 ($0.46/serving). Optimum Nutrition recommends you take two capsules twice daily since one serving (two capsules) only contains 2.5 grams of creatine.

That may not be a deterrent for some folks, but our team docked a few points off the formulation, giving Optimum Nutrition 3 out of 5 stars in this key category.

“You can always double the intake, but four pills is a lot and makes the serving size much more expensive,” our product tester noted.

Furthermore, our R.D. reviewer Anna Marie Clear notes: “A larger athlete (ie. 100 kilograms) would need to take eight capsules (10 grams of creatine) in order to meet the 1 gram per kilogram of body weight recommendation.” So if you’re a bigger person, you may want to opt for a powder that’s easier to take more of.

Recent findings suggest that these capsules have a simple ingredient list: creatine monohydrate, gelatin, and magnesium stearate. Magnesium stearate and gelatin form the capsule. Gelatin is an animal product, so these supplements are not vegan.

As for how easy they go down? Our product tester rated the swallowability 5 out of 5 stars.

“They are tasteless aside from a slight gelatin flavor,” he indicates. “And the pills are a bit large—about 1 inch long—but I didn’t have trouble swallowing them.”.

According to recent reports, if you’re trying to achieve some gnarly gains, you can’t go wrong with an affordably priced supplement made with the most widely used brand of creatine. Experts consider CreaPure®, a branded form of creatine monohydrate, the gold standard for purity and effectiveness. Nastasi agrees: “It’s manufactured in Germany and is super pure, so from a purity perspective it’s no. 1.”.

Industry observers note that gnarly is the only supplement on our list with this form of creatine. Each serving contains 5 grams of 100% CreaPure® creatine monohydrate, putting it ahead of the class and leading to a formulation score of 5 out of 5 stars. This research-backed dose can help support your physique-building efforts, as combining creatine supplementation with adequate resistance training is shown to be an effective muscle growth strategy.

According to recent reports, in addition, Gnarly Creatine is NSF Certified for Sport and NSF Content Certified. This means it’s third-party certified to be pure and free from banned substances. This is great news for athletes who compete in drug-tested athletic competitions, since testing positive for banned substances, even if they’re consumed by accident, can lead to disqualification. So, if you’re an aspiring bodybuilder looking to pack on as much muscle as possible, you don’t have to worry about any issues with Gnarly.

It has been revealed that “NSF Certified for Sport also indicates this supplement has undergone label claim testing (so the label is accurate) and contaminant testing for heavy metals, microbes, and pesticides,” says Clear. “This may be the most pure option on this list,” she adds.

While Gnarly earned a perfect third-party testing rating, it didn’t live up to our standards for solubility, leading to a disappointing score of 3 out of 5 stars.

“It doesn’t mix very well and settles quite a bit,” our product tester noted. “I usually end up stirring it several times while I take it.”Many Amazon reviews echo similar sentiments, so if you’re searching for a smooth sipping experience, consider an alternative like Sports Research.

Our team tested dozens of other creatines to come up with this list, with many of us relying on some form of this popular supplement for years. However, not every creatine product could make our list, so here are some honorable mentions that didn’t quite make the cut:.

Industry observers note that our team has tried more than 43 creatine supplements in total, with more added on the regular. We evaluate each supplement for the following factors:.

There are a few key factors you’ll want to consider when choosing a creatine supplement.

In a recent development, research shows the most efficacious dose of creatine is between 3 and 5 grams for most individuals. Look for supplements with servings within this range if you’re looking for maximum benefits, including increased muscle mass, faster recovery, and improved exercise capacity. Remember, larger individuals may require more creatine for maximum benefits—0.1 grams per kilogram of body weight is the research-backed recommendation.

Recent findings suggest that some supplements have additional ingredients to bolster the product’s effectiveness. Transparent Labs, for example, includes HMB, which some research shows promotes muscle growth, though more research is needed. Legion includes L-carnitine, which research shows helps metabolize fat into energy. Consider your goals and whether or not you want a pure creatine supplement or one with other athletic performance-enhancing ingredients.

“I highly recommend collaborating with a sports dietitian to find the most optimal supplement for you based on your personal health, athletic, or physique goals and to ensure you are consuming an appropriate dosage from a safe and high-quality supplement,” says Anna Marie Clear, our expert reviewer and R.D.

In a recent development, some creatine supplements use artificial ingredients and fillers to help improve taste and mixability. While many of the products on our list contain creatine as their sole ingredient, some, like Swoly gummies, use some artificial ingredients. Consider whether or not it’s vital for your supplement to be completely pure.

According to recent reports, third-party testing is the best way to ensure that your supplement’s ingredients are pure and match what’s on the label. Supplements are not regulated by the FDA, so third-party testing gives consumers confidence in their products.

“It is also especially crucial to consider third-party testing for sport certifications from either Informed Sport or NSF Certified for Sport if you are a collegiate or professional athlete or if you are looking to compete in a weightlifting, bodybuilding, or other fitness competition to ensure you are consuming supplements free from banned substances,” says Clear.

Industry observers note that creatine phosphate (CrP) is a compound made of three amino acids: arginine, glycine, and methionine. The body produces creatine naturally in the liver, kidneys, and pancreas, with about 95% of it found in skeletal muscle. “Through diet, creatine is found primarily in red meat and seafood, however, to get an extra creatine boost, a creatine powder or pill supplement can help,” says personal trainer and strength coach Will Duru.

Sources indicate that creatine supplies energy to muscles through the phosphocreatine system. “Creatine helps in the production of ATP (adenosine triphosphate)—the compound that provides energy to bodily processes such as muscle contraction,” nutritionist Rob Hobson indicates. “Creatine can help with the production of ATP during maximum-effort exercises, such as sprints or intense muscular effort lasting between five and 10 seconds. It can also help recovery between exercise bouts.”.

Hobson says creatine can improve performance in sports involving repeated sprints, such as rugby or football, and high-intensity bursts, like track or swim sprints. “Creatine can also help you train harder through being able to do more work over a series of training sets,” he adds.

As a certified personal trainer, former rugby player, and longtime lifter, I can attest to the impact that creatine has on both performance and recovery. It’s been a staple in my supplement stack for years, and despite myths about unwanted weight gain and water retention, I’ve never experienced those side effects.

As the most-researched supplement on the market, creatine has long been utilized by everyone from professional athletes to strength training enthusiasts to casual lifters. Let’s explore some of the positive potential effects of creatine supplementation:.

In a recent development, “Research highlights creatine supplementation helps muscle performance throughout a number of activities including soccer training, weight training, plyometric training, and even canoe training,” says Duru. Interestingly, this study also showed that muscle power output and muscle strength still increased with creatine supplementation, even when research subjects didn’t do any exercise. This is in comparison to subjects who took a placebo supplement.

In a recent development, “There are lots of studies showing how creatine supplementation can improve strength, power, and high-intensity exercise performance. This is due to the role it plays in energy production and its ability to increase ATP availability during short bursts of intense activity,” notes nutritionist Rob Hobson.

Industry observers note that want to build muscle? Creatine could be your go-to. “Creatine supplementation is often used to increase muscle mass. It can draw more water into your muscle cells, creating a cell volumization effect that may promote muscle growth,” says Hobson. “Additionally, creatine can enhance the effects of resistance training by increasing total muscle mass and strength gains.”.

According to a 2023 meta-analysis on the effects of creatine supplementation combined with resistance training, this protocol can promote “a small increase in the direct measures of skeletal muscle hypertrophy in both the upper and lower body.”.

Duru claims for maximum muscle-building results, creatine loading can help. “The first time you take creatine, take around 20 to 25 grams of creatine every day for up to a week, broken up into 5-gram servings across the day. Then drop to the recommended 3 to 5 grams the day after this.”.

Clear adds: “If you are looking to initiate creatine supplementation with a loading dose of 20 grams per day, I recommend breaking this large dosage into smaller servings throughout the day to minimize gastrointestinal distress (i.e., diarrhea).”.

Recovery is key when training. Not only does it help you avoid injury, but a speedier recovery means we can get back to exercise quicker. Research highlights creatine supplementation may reduce recovery time between spurts of intense exercise by reducing muscle damage.

Although supplementing with creatine does not entirely prevent muscle damage, studies show creatine reduces the immediate muscle damage that occurs after resistance training.

In a recent development, studies show creatine can benefit brain function. “Creatine supplementation may have a beneficial effect on brain function, as the brain requires a significant amount of ATP for normal operation. It may be particularly beneficial in tasks requiring speed and quick thinking,” states Hobson.

It has been revealed that creatine supplementation is also important for overall health and wellness as you age. According to a 2021 study led by renowned creatine researcher Dr. Darren Candow, one year of creatine supplementation and resistance training had favorable effects on bone area and muscle density in older adults. This included both male and female participants, suggesting no differences between sex when it comes to creatine’s impact.

Not all creatine is created equal. In fact, there are multiple forms. Here’s a brief overview of the different types of creatine so you understand what to look for and what might suit you best.

Creatine monohydrate consists of creatine paired with a water molecule. As nutritionist Rob Hobson notes, this is the most research-backed form of creatine, and it’s typically the primary form used in most of the best-selling supplements in this category.

“Micronized creatine is processed to create smaller particles than the standard creatine powder,” Hobson indicates. “The intention of micronized creatine is to improve its solubility and absorption in the body so creatine is then used up by muscles more quickly.”.

In this form, creatine is bound to ester salts, which some studies show makes the creatine more easily absorbed within the body. However, research demonstrates creatine ethyl ester is not as effective as monohydrate.

Sources indicate that creatine nitrate is derived from the same molecule as creatine monohydrate but with a nitrate added. Some studies suggest creatine nitrate is more bioavailable than monohydrate, but results are mixed and more research is needed. Right now, creatine nitrate is only approved by the FDA at a daily dose of 750 milligrams per day.

This type of creatine is normally manufactured with added alkaline, so it has a higher pH than regular creatine monohydrate. However, research shows there is little difference between buffered creatine and creatine monohydrate when it comes to training gains.

Sources indicate that A creatine loading phase involves taking a higher dose of creatine, typically between 20 and 25 grams, for up to a week, according to Duru. He recommends reducing to a dose of 3 to 5 grams a day after a week.

Sources indicate that “A lot of people do a creatine loading phase to fully saturate the muscles when they first start taking creatine, and this can potentially speed up the benefits by a few days,” states Pete Nastasi, CPT, CSNC. “But if you take more than two to three days off from creatine, it’s likely that your creatine stores will go back down to baseline and you might want to do another loading phase,” he says. “That’s why I suggest people take it every day.”.

According to recent reports, studies show creatine loading phases (e.g. 20 grams per day for five to seven days) can help increase muscle creatine storage by 10 to 30 percent. However, creatine loading phases aren’t necessary. Studies show that long term, you can achieve the same effects without a loading phase. But if it’s speed you’re after, loading phases are a safe and effective way to rapidly improve gains.

In a recent development, studies show creatine supplementation is safe in both the short and long term for healthy individuals. Healthy people can safely take up to 30 grams per day for up to five years. However, as we’ll explain below, those with certain health conditions should avoid creatine supplements.

“Since creatine is a safe supplement, there aren’t many precautions to take beyond sticking to the recommended dosage,” notes nutritionist Rob Hobson. “Like all supplements, figure out if it is really necessary to suit your performance goals, as there is little point in taking it if it is not. If you are training for a marathon then it’s not really going to be of use to you but if you are looking to build more muscle and become stronger, then it’s a good choice.”.

Creatine works for most people, but those with certain pre-existing health conditions should avoid it. “Anyone with pre-existing kidney or liver conditions or impaired function should avoid creatine,” says Hobson. Experts say creatine supplements may prevent those with kidney or liver problems from producing their own creatine. “Anyone taking medications affecting kidney function should avoid creatine or speak to their GP first. This might include blood pressure medication or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs on a regular basis,” Hobson adds.

Hobson also advises against creatine supplementation for those younger than 18. “With adolescents, while the research suggests it may be okay for this age group, I avoid recommending it as the long-term effects are not fully understood yet,” he says.

While myths exist about water retention, cramping, and even its legality, creatine is one of the most researched-backed supplements. If you’re a dedicated lifter looking to enhance your muscle gains, improve your performance in activities requiring short bursts of energy, or hasten your recovery, you shouldn’t hesitate to add one of the options from our list to your stack.

All you have to decide is whether you prefer a powder, pill, or gummy and you’ll be well on your way to unlocking the benefits of this uber-popular supplement.

Industry observers note that micronized creatine is processed to create smaller particles than the standard creatine powder. “Research reveals micronized creatine monohydrate is not any more bioavailable than creatine monohydrate itself,” states R.D. Anna Marie Clear.

According to recent reports, according to nutritionist Rob Hobson, most people take creatine after working out. “Research shows taking creatine after your workout may be marginally more beneficial given the increased uptake by muscles during this period, as exercise increases blood flow to muscle tissue,” he states.Hobson recommends taking creatine with a meal or a drink containing carbohydrates. “The effects of insulin help transport creatine into muscle cells,” he says.

According to recent reports, in short, no. According to the International Society of Sports Nutrition, “There is no scientific evidence that the short- or long-term use of creatine monohydrate has any detrimental effects on otherwise healthy individuals.”.

Sources indicate that research reveals the best dose is from 3 to 5 grams per day for most individuals. However, as R.D. Anna Marie Clear notes, the research-backed dose of 0.1 grams of creatine per kilogram of body weight means some larger individuals will need more than 5 grams per day to see optimal results.

Creatine may help increase your lean skeletal muscle mass, which can, in turn, increase your overall body weight. This overall increase in lean body mass will likely improve your body composition, as creatine supplementation does not impact your fat mass. “Good quality randomized controlled trials (one week to two years in duration) show creatine supplementation does not increase fat mass. Acute creatine supplementation (seven days) had no effect on fat mass in young and older adults; however, fat-free mass increased.”.

Industry observers note that when it comes to holiday gifts for the runner on your list, here’s the hard truth: No one needs another water bottle or foam roller. Instead, go bold and give shoes. But not just any pair. Choose ones that give their toes more room to move—and could make them a better runner by strengthening their feet.

According to recent reports, altra is famous for its roomy toe box, and here’s why that matters: Research found that wider designs better accommodate the foot’s natural shape than standard running shoes. That extra toe room can reduce stress on the feet and allow a fuller range of motion, reducing the risk of injuries not only in the feet, but also the lower back, hips, knees, and ankles.

Along with its signature Altra Fit (roomy toe box and low drop), Altra offers a model for nearly every fitness enthusiast on your list—including you. Here are some top options.

In a recent development, chilly mornings, humid evenings, slushy roads—when the daily run is a non-negotiable, there’s no such thing as bad weather, only the wrong shoes. The right ones are the Altra Experience Flow 3 GTX, with a waterproof upper to keep the feet dry and comfy and a grippy outsole for traction on wet surfaces. A low 4mm heel drop with a rocker shape adds a bit of propulsion, so your everyday runner can get more momentum with less effort.

Getting started can feel intimidating for many people, and the sheer breadth of gear choices adds to that overwhelm. Make it easy for the newbie on your holiday list and give the Altra Experience Flow 3, which has promptly become a fan favorite. The Experience Flow 3 is lightweight, bouncy, and stylish, and it also boasts a rocker shape geometry for a smooth heel-to-toe transition.

Recent findings suggest that seasoned runners often have two distinct categories of shoes: Ones for long training days and others for race day. The Altra Torin 9 does both jobs, making it a solid choice for the performance-seeking runner who appreciates the ability to wear the same shoes at any distance and still be comfortable. Responsive and soft, with a grippier outsole than the last version, this shoe combines two types of foam for stability and cushioning. There’s also an updated heel shape for improved fit, a secure midfoot that stays in place mile after mile, and the signature toe box that lets toes move freely. This is Altra’s longstanding, bestselling road shoe for a reason.

Recent findings suggest that trail running is experiencing a massive surge in popularity, with a recent report showing that U.S. participation has jumped by 57 percent since 2019. That means the trail runner on your list may be fresh to the sport, even if they’re not new to running. Because trails can be muddy, rocky, and root-laden, they require a specialized shoe like the Altra Experience Wild 3. Extra grippy for outdoor terrain while still being lightweight, the Wild 3 offers a rocker shape geometry and a super-practical GaiterTrap—a built-in attachment system that allows trail gaiters to lock onto the back of the shoe. There’s also room for the toes while still having the secure midfoot for natural movement around all those trail obstacles.

If your giftee has been conquering terrain for years, they’ve probably heard about the Altra Lone Peak 9, the shoe that put Altra on the map for trail running. It’s been Altra’s bestselling trail shoe for over a decade, and each version gets better. This ninth generation has been reengineered for more durability, with a revised midsole foam that offers lighter weight than previous iterations. A roomy toe box, space through the midfoot, ripstop mesh upper for high-mileage performance, and ultrasticky grip in practically all conditions? Legendary.

Many gym goers like to warm up with a treadmill session before transitioning into strength work, and that usually requires a shoe change. Not anymore. The Altra Escalante 5 is the brand’s beloved cross-trainer, and it shifts from running to lifting like a pro athlete. Strength training shoes require less soft arch support and cushioning because their main job is to provide stability rather than to absorb impact. The Escalante 5 has a low stack height, streamlined design, and zero drop. That keeps the feet completely flat, mimicking a natural barefoot position favored by serious lifters, while still providing good lateral support for cross-training and functional workouts.

Packing multiple shoes for a vacation or business trip is about as appealing as trying to sneak liquids past airport security. If your gift recipient is the type who looks for a run soon after stepping off the plane, there’s the Altra FWD VIA 2. Softer and more responsive than the previous version of the model, it also boasts a mesh upper for increased breathability, a roomy toe box, and rocker shape geometry. Whether someone is running through the airport, sightseeing for hours, or putting a workout on the vacay itinerary, this is the perfect travel partner.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, they say pride comes before the fall. In cycling, I’ve found pride usually comes before the first true descent.

Sources indicate that I relearned this lesson earlier this month, when I found myself at the top of Bear Mountain, the only notable multi-mile climb close enough to bike to from New York City. Its peak was situated about halfway into the 105-mile route of the Best Buddies Challenge New York, an event the organization had brought back for a second year to fund its programming for teenagers and young adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities. The riders gawking at the intermittently vermilion canopy who were pedaling alongside me had each raised at least $1,800 to reach this particular vista, plus access to several deliciously well-stocked aid stations, SAG vehicles, and the promise of a raucous finish-line party.

Though I’m relatively latest to road cycling, I’ve done some long gravel rides and recently tackled the Maratona dles Dolomites in Italy, where I buried myself to finish a 66-mile route that featured over 10,000 feet of elevation and one 8-mile climb up the Passo Valparolo. By comparison, the Best Buddies Challenge century, with 2,000 fewer feet of climbing stretched over a much longer route, seemed plenty doable when I signed up in September.

The first indication I had erred came before I had pinned my bib number to my jersey. At a pre-ride reception, I sat down with Alberto Contador (yes, that Alberto Contador), who was returning to the event for the second time. He was confident I could handle Bear Mountain, but warned me that the end of the ride reminded him of La Flèche Wallonne, a notoriously difficult Belgian one-day race known for its repeat ascents of the relatively short, brutally steep Mur de Huy. “The last 30 miles is all up and down…save energy,” he stated.

In a recent development, by the time I slid into the fourth aid station, which marked the 33-miles-to-go point in my own ride, this advice was well out of my mind. I was supremely confident in my ability to finish strong. Sure, I had gone a bit deeper in the tank to maintain contact with random groups throughout the day in valleys and on shallow sections, but there was so little left to go.

How hard could the rest really be?

The Best Buddies Challenge is relatively new to New York City, but the concept of the charity ride is not. The Five Boro Bike Tour, which raises money for Bike New York’s free education and mechanics program, has given city cyclists the chance to experience streets without car traffic since 1977. On the West Coast, Washington’s Cascade Bicycle Club’s Seattle to Portland Bicycle Classic now generates about $1 million each year to fund the organization’s community programs, cycling education, and statewide cycling advocacy work. Even the ride I did in the Dolomites this summer offers charity entrants, who have, over the years, raised over $2 million for road safety, food security, disease research, and rural education.

It has been revealed that among non-endurance athletes, these rides often draw comparisons to running events like the Upcoming York City Marathon. There are certainly similarities—sanctioned routes, feed stations, distances that sound absurd to normies—but cyclists don’t tend to give even long charity rides anything close to the same level of credence as runners do to marathons.

Sources indicate that that kind of resistance perhaps comes from those strains of cycling tradition that prize grit and ardor and self-reliance. Conquering Mur de Huy during a race takes superhuman levels of tenacity and determination—charity rides, by contrast, even those that span 100 miles, are much more comfortable affairs. Do some riders dismiss these events because they’re too soft? It’s possible.

Beginner-friendliness is often baked into the event programming of charity rides. Breakthrough T1D Rides, held to fund research for type 1 diabetes, are actually four-day retreats. Participants spend only one day on the bike. Anthony Geraci, national director of Ride & Endurance Programs, notes most of these rides feature “out-and-back” courses. Turn around whenever you feel done with your day! “We always say it’s not about the miles, it’s about the mission.”.

Industry observers note that sure, you could cross-stitch that phrase onto a throw pillow. But it’s also the kind of mentality that cyclists might need to achieve some personal goals, whether that’s riding in a newly introduced destination or tackling their first century. In this way, charity rides can be catalysts for remarkable personal achievement.

They also create the conditions for extremely impressive fundraising. Best Buddies International CEO Anthony Shriver (yes, that Shriver) told me that its cycling events account for about 10 to 15 percent of the organization’s annual revenue. Similarly, Kris Rauh, vice president, event experience and operations for NMSS, says its 49 Bike MS events generate about $52 million in revenue annually for the organization.

Sources indicate that indeed, she continued, many of the people signing up to do their first Bike MS have no personal connection to the disease in its name. “They come to us mostly because they want a challenge on a bike … they don’t come to us as fundraisers,” she said.

For charity rides like Bike MS and Best Buddies, it’s key to connect participants to their mission and the impact of their work. As I ascended Bear Mountain and pushed myself on the way back, I wasn’t just riding with Contador and Chris Froome (who was also participating this year) but also plenty of folks who volunteer for or participate in Best Buddies programming. In fact, individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities often held key roles during its rides. At the Challenge Upcoming York, a “Buddy” gave a speech while we waited in the start pen, a different “Buddy” sang the national anthem, and still others staffed the aid stations. “From the moment you wake up at 4 o’clock in the morning, you should know you’re doing something that’s going to enrich another human being’s life,” Shriver noted.

Sources indicate that the combination makes these kinds of charity rides feel a lot different than a standard criterium or gravel fondo. And it seems to hold enough appeal to keep the organizations hosting them going. Best Buddies, which has substantial fundraising minimums for riders, gets a 30 to 50 percent return rate, Shriver indicates. According to Rauh, at Bike MS that number is closer to 60 percent. That’s a lot of people returning to charity rides each year.

About two-thirds of the way into my own Upcoming York Challenge, I was actively questioning how this could be possible. Though I had been correct that all the long climbs were behind me, the “rolling” terrain I had imagined was actually a freak show of sharp pitches. I cracked on a climb my Garmin did not categorize, attempting to hold serve over a bump with a gradient of 18 percent.

Sources indicate that I unclipped and shuffled my cramping legs up the embarrassingly short walk to the summit. I felt ashamed by the level of hubris I had brought into the event. If it had been just a regular ride, or even a race, this might have been my day. With hours left to a finish that I felt confident most of the participants had already crossed, it would have been totally within my prerogative to pull the quick-release lever off my front wheel and stuff my bike in a Lyft bound back to Brooklyn.

Industry observers note that but as I munched on some blissfully salty crackers that quieted my screaming hamstrings, I realized that getting to the end would be an accomplishment for me regardless of how fast I was able to do it. And, importantly, my path to the shuttle bus that would take me back to the city included one final rest stop. Resolved never to underestimate a “ride” again, I got back in the saddle and held the limpest zone 1 pace of my life until I had made it to the aforementioned support tent. With less than 10 miles left, I slumped into a folding chair and sucked down a can of Sprite.

In a recent development, immediately, I was engaged by Matt, who was participating in the ride as a volunteer. He asked if I was okay, and when it was clear that I was mentally wrecked, but physically fine, gently encouraged me to get moving. With Matt, another volunteer named Ian, and a pair of other riders who had also had similarly tough days, we set off on the last stretch to the end.

It has been revealed that chatting in my bunch, really the only bunch I had been able to hang on to the entire day, made the miles go by faster and the remaining climbs feel shorter. And when the sugar from my soda hit, I realized I was actually less dead than the pair of participants I had just encountered. Ian and I forged ahead, buoyed by the knowledge the end was near. I managed to stay upright enough up the finishing hill to attempt a celebratory pose as I crossed over the finish line: ninth to last. It was the longest ride I’ve ever done and it challenged me to push myself harder than I might otherwise have done. That’s worth something.

Does anyone have a cool $2,000 I could use to try again next year?

#217310. I Thought I Was Getting Slower Because of Age. Then an Incidental Scan Revealed the Real Problem—and Likely Saved My Life.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2816 w)
📖 Baca

I Thought I Was Getting Slower Because of Age. Then an Incidental Scan Revealed the Real Problem—and Likely Saved My Life.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2816 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, last year, a lung scan—ordered even though I’d ground out my last butt decades earlier—incidentally picked up a bulge in my aorta.
  • I was in my mid-fifties and healthy.
  • Industry observers note that further tests revealed the diameter of my aorta to be twice the normal size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smoking may have saved my life.

In a recent development, last year, a lung scan—ordered even though I’d ground out my last butt decades earlier—incidentally picked up a bulge in my aorta. Because I smoked heavily when I was young, my doctor sent me for a screening after the age eligibility had been lowered, just in case. While the scan didn’t find any signs of cancer, it detected something else. An aneurysm: a weak spot in the body’s main artery that causes it to balloon.

I was baffled. I was in my mid-fifties and healthy. I had no family history of cardiovascular issues. I was a longtime runner. I ate my veggies and hadn’t had a drink in 27 years. My resting heart rate was borderline smug.

Industry observers note that further tests revealed the diameter of my aorta to be twice the normal size. Putting me at risk of an aortic dissection or rupture, both life-threatening emergencies that demand immediate treatment.

Recent findings suggest that damn. How long had I been walking—and running—around with this fault line trembling in my chest?

While waiting for an appointment with a cardiologist, I was seized with anxiety. I stopped exercising. I practiced randomly unlocking the emergency feature on my phone and rapidly making a mental note of my location.

According to recent reports, an echocardiogram later revealed that the bulge had also pulled apart the leaflets of my aortic valve, preventing them from sealing tightly. With every heartbeat, some of the blood my heart pumped out leaked backward, forcing it to work harder to circulate the same blood twice.

“Given that you’re only in your fifties and live an active lifestyle,” the cardiologist said, “I’d suggest you consult with a cardiac surgeon.”.

In a recent development, the last sentence I thought I’d ever hear. Until I was met with, “Let’s schedule you for open-heart surgery.”.

In a recent development, looking back, I wondered if there had been signs. I had tried to run at least one marathon or ultra a year, along with some shorter distances. In recent years, no matter how hard I trained, I could never improve my times, my marathons creeping up from low four hours to a whisper below five. I increasingly had to run/walk the final miles. I tried a vegan diet to improve my energy and switched to forefoot running for more spring in my stride. Nothing budged. Maybe I was just getting older.

Gradually, and then seemingly all at once, running became a grind. I started cutting workouts short. The hills felt steeper. The part I looked forward to most was stopping. The joy I had always found in movement was supplanted by fatigue and frustration and more frequent visits to my physical therapist. After plodding across the finish line at the 2025 Falmouth Road Race, I hit the pause button and wondered if I’d ever press play again.

Industry observers note that running has been part of my identity for most of my adult life. After years of flailing, it showed me I was capable. It soothed the anxieties of sobriety and helped me believe I was more than the drunken jerk many people knew when I was in my teens and twenties. It was a sandbox for role-playing difficult conversations, reckoning with my trespasses, and cultivating humility. It was where the idea for my first book took shape and stories took root. It was a way to find people like me, if only through those knowing waves as we passed. Running was more than a healthy habit. It was a partner, my better half.

Industry observers note that after all these years, had I fallen out of love? And if I had, who would I be without it?

Open-heart surgery involves slicing through the chest, sawing the sternum in two, parting the halves with a retractor, and stopping the heart. The task of keeping you alive is outsourced to a machine. Even though doctors have been successfully performing this procedure for decades, when it’s you going up on that table, it feels like science fiction.

Recent findings suggest that as the date of my surgery crept closer, fear and anxiety filled me like a helium balloon. The idea of intubation kept me up at night. What if I wake gagging and rip the tube out?

The mortality rate was one in a hundred.

It has been revealed that I calmed myself the way I would before a big race: meditation, yoga, and Peggy Huddleston’s pre-surgery relaxation techniques. I studied “the course” and sought out people who’d been through it, looking for any kind of mental edge. And though I was not a religious person, I asked friends and family for prayers, having read that they’d been shown to influence outcomes.

Recent findings suggest that early one morning in February, I was wheeled into an operating bay at Massachusetts General Hospital, knocked unconscious and chemically paralyzed. Over the next five hours, my surgeon removed my diseased aortic root and ascending aorta, replaced them with a synthetic graft and carbon valve, and hooked my coronary arteries back up to the newly introduced plumbing.

When they took me off bypass, my heart forgot how to beat. Instead of pumping, it quivered, seized by electrical chaos. Ventricular fibrillation. The doctors had to shock my heart back into rhythm. Four times. Inside the cardiac OR, the team was ready. Anywhere else, it would have been goodnight, Irene.

I knew none of this when I groggily opened my eyes in the ICU that evening. I felt trampled. I could see the breathing tube that had haunted me for weeks protruding from my mouth, my hands bound to the bedrail to keep me from reaching for it, but I felt no urge, couldn’t feel it. The second time I woke up—the first just brief enough to realize where I was—a voice said, “Squeeze my hand.” My eyelids too heavy to lift, I managed, then drifted back into blackness. When I stirred again, the tube was gone. Relief. But drainage lines snaked from my chest into canisters, while wires and catheters tethered me to a forest of blinking monitors.

In a recent development, later, in the step-down cardiac ward, I needed a walker to cover even the shortest distance, the drainage boxes hanging on the sides like hard saddlebags. I was carrying 15 extra pounds of fluid, my fingers fat as cocktail wieners. I shuffled down the hall in grippy socks, a tech beside me and a chair trailing behind should I need to sit.

I spent a week at Mass General, three months of recovery ahead of me. In the early weeks, the focus was on walking. Three minutes at a time. Twice a day. Getting to the end of the block took effort. My wife (stone-cold angel!) set up chairs on the landing so I could stop and catch my breath going upstairs in our house outside of Boston. Instead of crushing miles, I was crushing naps.

At six weeks, I met with my surgeon for a follow-up. She was pleased with my progress and lifted some restrictions and cleared me for cardiac rehab. She showed me a picture of my valve leaflets riddled with holes. Told me the aneurysm had likely been there for a decade, the aortic wall “paper thin.” I felt dizzy as if peering over the edge of a tall building. You hear about runners collapsing at the end of marathons, about shovelers going down after a snowstorm. Had it only been a matter of time?

Recent findings suggest that as she described the repair—a Bentall procedure, one of the more complex operations in cardiac surgery—a seductive thought wormed its way into my brain. Sure, aging may have started to slow me down, but a leaky, punctured valve must have been robbing my body of strength and energy, too. Now that a set of brand-new carbon leaflets was opening and closing tightly, blood safely moving in the right direction, could I get my running back on track? Maybe emerge stronger and faster, start breaking PRs again. Could I fall back in love?

I stared at my surgeon, the woman who had held my heart in her hands. Had she seen that old spark still flickering in there?

Cardiac rehab is part safety net, part exercise boot camp. A mini gym with EKG leads and blood-pressure cuffs. When I walked in, an elderly woman in jeans pedaled a recumbent bike while a silver-haired man in a rugby shirt and mask worked an arm cycle. Nearby, an old man plucked one of the resistance ropes that hung from hooks like a swarm of eels. Not everyone had undergone surgery. Some were recovering from heart attacks or stent procedures, others from dangerous arrhythmias or heart failure. I didn’t see anyone else my age.

A physical therapist named Andi asked about my surgery and fitness history, then my goals.

“The seven-mile Falmouth Road Race in four months,” I said. Returning a year later, with a sternum fused by wire, felt like a symbolic milestone. For good measure, I added, “and a marathon next spring.”.

Industry observers note that I leaned back, waiting for her eyes to light up with amazement. I bet she didn’t hear that very often. She kept scribbling. Probably too stunned, I figured.

Sources indicate that she handed me a laminated workout card. “No treadmill?” I frowned. “Soon. Let’s see how you do with these exercises.”.

It has been revealed that I climbed onto a stationary bike and quietly turned the resistance a few notches above the prescribed setting. I watched my heart rate climb on the monitor above the nurse’s station: 100, 110, 120. Sweat prickled my forehead. That old feeling. For almost two months, my body had belonged to surgeons, nurses, and restrictions. Now, little by little, it would be returned to its rightful owner.

Andi kept her promise. A few weeks later, she prescribed one minute of running. Sixty seconds at a 14-minute pace, followed by two minutes of walking. Five intervals. Three-quarters of a mile. The longest I’d run in eight months. It felt every bit as satisfying as finishing a marathon.

In a recent development, as I built from one-minute intervals to two, then three, I stopped thinking so much about future PRs and training plans. I was running again. The minutes stretched. The walks grew shorter. The weeks passed. By the third month, I was running two miles continuously and sweating so much that the EKG leads kept popping off my chest. Andi would laugh and hand me a fresh set.

It has been revealed that when I arrived, I’d seen those sticky leads as signs that I was still a patient. Now they wouldn’t stay on, blanking out my little section on the wall monitor.

It has been revealed that on August 16, 2026, I stood among the heaving throngs on Water Street in Woods Hole, the staging area for the Falmouth Road Race on Cape Cod. I stroked my chest. Still tender six months later. Amid shouts and laughter, selfies and the sharp medicinal smell of Bengay mixed with sunscreen, my mind hummed with questions: Was I still the runner I used to be? Did we have a future together? Had my slump been caused by my heart—or “my heart?”.

Every few minutes, the crowd surged forward, then stopped, then surged again—an electrical current passing through thousands of bodies as waves of runners were slowly released onto the course.

At last we crossed the starting line. As I set off, an old familiar voice rose to taunt me: This doesn’t count as your big comeback if you take walk breaks, and Dave McGillivray ran the entire Boston Marathon six months after heart surgery.

But then the race gave me something else to listen to. The pounding of rubber soles like golf applause. Spectators shaking cowbells and waving signs. The theme song from “Rocky” pouring from unseen speakers at Nobska Light. The cheers rose around us, and somewhere beyond them the waters of Vineyard Sound flashed in the sun, the island a squiggle on the horizon. Then an emptiness settled over the salty air.

Sources indicate that I found myself thinking about who I had become. Or maybe who I’d spent my adult life trying to become. The abstinent runner. The marathoner chasing his father’s PR. The ultrarunner. The trail runner, leaping logs and picking my way across rocks with my trusty dog trotting beside me. Every few years, another version of myself to reel in.

Maybe, for the first time, I needed to stop fishing for some future version of myself. Maybe that was the gift of starting over: the chance to be a beginner again. Who I was 20 years ago. The overweight lug, freshly sober, shuffling down a dirt road in Vermont in the predawn blackness, listening to cicadas and coyotes, watching for flattened frogs and gravel stones the size of baby shoes. The accretion of feeling, competence, and the desire to be a better person. I didn’t know what a PR was. Or a starting corral. My finish line was the sunrise over the Green Mountains. Something I could never reach, only watch in awe. Back when distant light was all I needed.

Industry observers note that every few miles of the race, I walked for a minute. No earbuds. A friend ran beside me, an easy presence, and we chatted, and sometimes we didn’t. The race was everything I’d hoped it would be, which is to say: nothing. No expectations. No aspirations. Pace didn’t matter. I only checked my watch to make sure my heart rate didn’t climb above 180. Falmouth reminded me of a few things: that we are remarkably resilient, that the ocean never fails to awe, and, according to one spectator’s sign, that you should never “trust a fart after mile 6.”.

It has been revealed that when I crossed the finish line, I raised my arms perfunctorily and smiled for the photographers, lifting my shirt to flash my scar like I was at Mardi Gras. But on the drive home, the emptiness lingered. No epiphany. No transformation. No cinematic moment of rebirth.

Recent findings suggest that I had run seven miles. And somehow, that was all.

Industry observers note that that old blah feeling persisted. It took me longer to get out the door, my pace stuck in the basement. So I put a half marathon on the books.

Sources indicate that A rare fall nor’easter blew into town one Friday and was still raging on Sunday: rain and wind blowing sideways, tree branches nearly horizontal, deck furniture scattered. I was behind in my training and needed to get a long run in that weekend. I hemmed and hawed for a couple of hours, hoping it would let up. It didn’t.

Finally, I got dressed. My Garmin had died the week before, so I set off blind. No pace, distance, or heart-rate information. By the time I reached the bike path along the Charles, my clothes were plastered to my skin. Broken branches and leaves littered the pavement. It looked like the aftermath of a house party. Rain hammered the river. With a playlist in my ears, I felt as if I were running through an adventure movie.

Sources indicate that cars sent waves of water rolling over the guardrails. Enormous puddles swamped the path. At first I tried to avoid them. Then I realized there was no point, and it became fun. I splashed through them like a kid.

It has been revealed that I was the only one out there. Despite the wild weather, everything felt quiet, abandoned. And somehow that spurred me on. A small tree had fallen across a wooden footbridge. I had to wrestle it out of the way. Storylines bubbled up. I was racing to the next town after a catastrophic event, seeking help; lives depended on me. I had to keep going.

Finally, I saw another runner, both of us looking like we’d been fished out of a lake. We waved—not perfunctorily, but with a knowing look. Was he running for help, too?

Industry observers note that the slap of my feet on wet asphalt took over the soundtrack, along with the gusts of my own breathing and the faint ticking of my mechanical valve in my throat. I had no idea how far I’d gone or how much farther I had to go.

For once, I didn’t need to know. I felt inside and outside everything at the same time, the rain somehow lighting the way.

Caleb Daniloff is a Boston-area writer and author of Running Ransom Road: Confronting The Past One Marathon at a Time and co-author of November Project: The Book: Inside the Free Grassroots Fitness Movement That’s Taking Over The World.

Industry observers note that whether you’re starting your fitness journey or you’re a weightlifting junkie, there are several supplements that should be staples in your stack. Then, with some guidance from a few other experts, our squad of CPTs, CNCs, CrossFit enthusiasts, and dedicated weightlifters narrowed down the list to the eight strongest pre-workouts so you can select the perfect match for your goals and preferences.

Medical disclaimer: This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any upcoming supplement or exercise regimen.

If your goal is to improve your athletic performance and power output in the gym, then we recommend Transparent Labs BULK BLACK. And studies show betaine anhydrous may improve muscular endurance. These ingredients work together to enhance your training, paving the way for strength gains over time.

Sources indicate that each serving of BULK BLACK also contains 350 milligrams of caffeine, which is close to the recommended daily limit of 400 milligrams. Overall, the impressive formulation earns 4 out of 5 stars from our team, as we docked a point for the high caffeine content since it may be too intense for some people.

Cory also experienced the tingling sensation common with high doses of beta-alanine.

Sources indicate that cory also enjoys using BULK BLACK before bodybuilding workouts since it contains 8,000 milligrams of citrulline malate. While more research is needed, some studies suggest citrulline malate may boost exercise and muscular performance.

Two other areas where BULK BLACK stands out: solubility and taste. Our team gave Transparent Labs perfect scores in both categories.

“It’s hard to describe the taste of Blue Raspberry, but that’s exactly what it tastes like. Not too sweet, which is a good thing,” he notes.

Legion Pulse is our pick for the strongest natural pre-workout because it’s free from artificial sweeteners, flavors, and colors and contains six active ingredients that support enhanced energy.

Sources indicate that as a CPT and CNC, I look for four main ingredients in a high-quality pre-workout supplement: caffeine, beta-alanine, betaine anhydrous, and L-citrulline. Each plays a key role in enhancing athletic performance. Research demonstrates:.

Legion Pulse contains all four, including 350 milligrams of caffeine per serving, which is very close to the recommended daily limit of 400 milligrams. Keep in mind that if you decide to try Pulse, it’s a good idea to monitor your caffeine intake from other sources like coffee or tea.

Recent findings suggest that “To get the most out of pre-workout supplements without stomach issues, start with a lower dose to see how your body reacts,” says Dr. Christopher Mohr, Ph.D., RD. “Choose supplements with fewer stimulants if caffeine bothers you, or go for stimulant-free options.”.

Luckily, if you’re upcoming to pre-workout or are caffeine-sensitive, you can also choose the non-stim version of Pulse. So, even though we’d like to see creatine in the formulation, we still give this a strong score of 4 out of 5 stars, especially since there’s a caffeine-free version.

While the formulation and flavor options make this a top-rated pre-workout, Pulse is by no means a budget-friendly option. At around $45 for a 20-serving tub, it earns the lowest score of 1 out of 5 stars for price per serving.

While many strong pre-workouts cost around $2 per serving, Nutricost Pre-X is our pick for the strongest budget pre-workout because it costs less than half of that. At about $0.93 per serving, one tester called it “the best value on the market,” and I agree, giving this a perfect score of 5 out of 5 for price per serving.

Although some budget pre-workouts lack key ingredients, Pre-X contains the four main ones we like to see in a pre-workout: caffeine, beta-alanine, betaine anhydrous, and L-citrulline. “The price is better than most other pre-workouts I’ve tried, especially for a supplement this good,” says one tester.

Sources indicate that each serving of Pre-X has 300 milligrams of caffeine and 4,000 milligrams of L-citrulline, so you should feel energized and get a good pump with this pre-workout. “I got a decent pump and had a calm focus without feeling overstimulated,” one tester notes.

Some testers say Pre-X has a slightly lower dosage of beta-alanine than some other pre-workouts on our list, but others say they experienced noticeable tingles during their workout.

While testers did not experience any negative side effects when trying Pre-X, this pre-workout is made with the artificial sweetener sucralose. Some health experts have raised concerns about taking sucralose in high doses. As a CPT and someone who pays close attention to everything I put in my body, I tend to steer clear of artificial sweeteners. Because of this, we docked a point off the formulation score, giving Pre-X 4 out of 5 stars.

Nutricost Pre-X comes in five flavors, including Blue Raspberry, Peach Mango, and Watermelon. Collectively, our team gave this strong pre-workout 4.5 out of 5 stars for taste.

“This tastes great ice cold or at room temperature. I look forward to drinking it before my workouts,” claims one tester who tried Blue Raspberry.

Another tester who tried Peach Mango also gave Pre-X his stamp of approval.

“No artificial sweetener taste at all. It has a nice flavor that’s not overly sweet.”.

Recent findings suggest that whether you like a strong pre-workout that’s sweet, sour, fruity, or tart, Jacked Factory NitroSurge has a fit for you. With 11 options, you can stick to your favorite or keep a few flavors in rotation to keep your taste buds on their proverbial toes. Between the deep lineup and satisfying flavors, NitroSurge earned a perfect score for taste.

One of our testers tried Strawberry Margarita, and let’s just say she was more than satisfied with her sipping experience.

Industry observers note that “It’s wildly delicious. I’d drink this by the side of the pool over ice all day.”.

According to recent reports, another tester prefers Jacked Factory NitroSurge to some other strong pre-workouts he’s tried. “I did not like the Pink Lemonade flavor of Legion Pulse, but I would definitely use the Grape NitroSurge again,” he notes.

As for its effectiveness? For one of our product testers, it took about 20 minutes to feel NitroSurge kick in. At that point, he felt like he could lift harder.

“I usually work out in the morning because I feel most rested then, but even after taking this in the afternoon, I felt ‘jacked up’ and ready to go,” he indicates, adding that he experienced tingles and a slight drop off, but neither was overwhelming.

Industry observers note that another tester who regularly takes strong pre-workouts doubled the dosage. He stated he got “a bit of a boost from it” but nothing like what you’ll get from other strong pre-workouts. Ultimately, this makes NitroSurge a solid choice for beginners, as you can see how you respond to a single serving before upping it to two scoops.

Recent findings suggest that besides the taste, I like that it’s budget-friendly while still including evidence-backed ingredients, like L-citrulline, beta-alanine, betaine anhydrous, caffeine anhydrous, L-theanine, theobromine, and AstraGin. AstraGin, also found in Transparent Labs BULK BLACK, is a plant-based compound formulated to enhance nutrient absorption. While AstraGin is safe at 0.5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day, more research is needed on the potential performance-enhancing benefits.

It has been revealed that like some of the other pre-workouts on our list, NitroSurge is made with the artificial sweetener sucralose, which some health experts have raised concerns about taking in high doses. Also, Jacked Factory supplements do not undergo third-party testing, which ensures products include the ingredients listed on the label and nothing else. This is especially key for athletes who undergo drug testing for banned substances. We only gave Nitrosurge 3 out of 5 stars in this category since it is made in a Current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP)-certified and FDA-registered facility.

For bodybuilders, a “pump” is a sign of a successful training session. Increased blood flow to the muscles makes them feel fuller and appear larger and more vascular during and after a workout. A pump also promotes muscle growth by delivering essential nutrients and oxygen to the muscles as blood flow increases. While you can achieve a pump through high-rep sets, drop sets, and supersets, high-stim pre-workouts like Gorilla Mode are specially designed to improve your pump.

Sources indicate that gorilla Mode contains several pump-enhancing ingredients in each scoop, including 5,000 milligrams of pure L-citrulline (more per scoop than any other pre-workout on our list) and 2,000 milligrams of Hydro Prime glycerol powder. L-citrulline works to widen blood vessels, increasing blood flow to the muscles. Glycerol powder is rapidly absorbed by the muscles and draws in water, which can cause muscle cell swelling.

In a recent development, if you’re caffeine-sensitive or budget-conscious, this intense pre-workout may not be the best for you. Although one serving only contains 200 milligrams of caffeine, you will need to take two servings to get research-backed doses of some key ingredients, including creatine monohydrate (only 2.5 gram per serving). At that point, you’d be at 400 milligrams of caffeine, which is the total amount the FDA says is safe for adults to consume per day. For this reason, we docked a point off the formulation, giving Gorilla Mode 4 out of 5 stars in this category.

Don’t forget that this also impacts how much bang you get for your buck. A 40-serving tub costs $60, and you’ll end up going through it that much quicker if you take two scoops before your training sessions. That would bring the cost to $3 per serving. So, from a value standpoint, we can only give Gorilla Mode 2.5 out of 5 stars.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, this pricey supplement earned a strong score of 4.5 out of 5 stars for its effectiveness. One of our testers uses strong pre-workouts several times a week and tried Gorilla Mode before an upper-body workout. “Not only did I have a good pump, I also felt more focused. I knocked out a few more reps than usual during my workout,” he says. “I like the Fruit Punch flavor, although it was sweeter than I thought it would be.”.

According to recent reports, while our tester enjoyed Gorilla Mode’s taste, he says the powder was gritty and difficult to mix properly. This is likely due to the glycerol powder, which absorbs moisture, leading to clumping.

If you like feeling skin tingles after taking your pre-workout, check out Crazy Nutrition Intensive Pre-Train. I love the prickly skin sensation because it lets me know my pre-workout is kicking in and it’s time to train. This temporary side effect, called paresthesia, is caused by beta-alanine, which works to increase muscular endurance.

Intensive Pre-Train has 3,500 milligrams of beta-alanine per serving, which is more per serving than almost all of the other pre-workouts on our list. “Beta-alanine is found in most pre-workout supplements, likely because it helps reduce fatigue and improve endurance in the short term,” says registered dietitian Alex Oskian. “This is because it reduces acidity in the body, which comes from lactic acid build-up.”.

Our product tester used Crazy Nutrition Intensive Pre-Train before a high-intensity interval training (HIIT) workout and felt the tingles within 15 minutes. “These were strong compared to some other pre-workouts I’ve tried,” he states. “I felt good tingles in my hands and face, which lasted for about an hour.”.

In a recent development, earning a 5 out of 5 for effectiveness, Intense Pre-Train is also available in a caffeine-free version for those who don’t want stimulants in their pre-workout. The non-stim version comes in Green Apple, which our tester claims tasted more like a greens powder than a sour apple.

Industry observers note that “I’m rather caffeine-dependent, so I didn’t feel a burst of energy. I prefer caffeinated pre-workouts, but this is a great option for a late-night lifting session,” she says. Other testers who tried the Fruit Punch flavor say they enjoyed the tangy taste. To enhance the flavor, Crazy Nutrition is sweetened with the artificial sweetener sucralose. With some mixed reviews on the different flavors, we give this pre-workout a 3.5 out of 5 for taste.

Onnit Alpha Brain is designed to increase mental acuity and focus. Testers say that’s exactly how they felt after trying Onnit Alpha Brain, which is why it’s our pick for the strongest pre-workout for focus.“What makes this pre-workout stand out is the cognitive effects. I felt significantly more focused after taking Alpha Brain than any other pre-workout I’ve tried,” notes one of our testers.

Other testers agreed, saying Alpha Brain helped them feel present and ready to work out without being overstimulated, leading to an effectiveness score of 4 out of 5 stars.

It has been revealed that onnit Alpha Brain’s formula differs from most other strong pre-workout supplements on our list — it contains nootropics, substances that enhance learning and memory. One of the key ingredients, NooGandha, is an ashwagandha extract that can reduce stress and enhance well-being by reducing cortisol levels in the body.

Another key ingredient, AlphaSize, may promote the production of acetylcholine, a powerful neurotransmitter that enhances cognitive function. However, studies demonstrating the effect of alpha-GPC on cognitive performance used 200 to 400 milligram doses per day, and a serving of Onnit Alpha brain has 125 milligrams.

The other unique ingredient in Onnit Alpha Brain is Dynamine. It works similarly to caffeine, by blocking the body’s adenosine receptors that cause you to feel tired. However, this ingredient is banned in all sports supplements in Australia. While Dynamine is still allowed for sports competitions in the U.S., it is possible it will be banned in the future. Competitive athletes may want to steer clear of this product.

Industry observers note that one of our testers claims Alpha Brain is only middle-of-the-road compared to other strong pre-workouts when it comes to physical energy. “After taking other strong pre-workouts, I usually experience a boost in energy. After taking this pre-workout, the mental effects were much more noticeable than the physical ones,” she says. That may be in part because Alpha Brain lacks ingredients like betaine anhydrous, taurine, and creatine, which can support muscle growth and recovery.

We give the formulation 4 out of 5 stars thanks to the inclusion of nootropics, which are promptly becoming more prevalent in the supplement market. But be aware that this probably isn’t your best bet for boosting your physical energy levels.

Long before the days of gummy and ready-to-drink (RTD) pre-workout options, the most popular choice was the original C4. The latest version, C4 Ultimate, is more concentrated than the classic formula, combining both exercise performance and cognitive-enhancing ingredients.

One of our testers tried C4 Ultimate before a 30-minute HIIT workout, reporting that the caffeine blend got her zoned in before her training.

“I felt great throughout the entire workout,” she reported, giving C4 Ultimate a perfect score for effectiveness.

According to recent reports, this high-stim pre-workout is sweetened with sucralose, which some health experts have raised concerns about. While our tester doesn’t mind a very sweet pre-workout, the Icy Blue Razz flavor was a little too sugary for her liking. Mixing it in more water than recommended balances out the sweetness.

However, another tester was blown away by the Sour Batch Bros flavor, saying it tasted “just like Sour Patch Kids.” Taking both of their experiences into consideration, we’ll meet in the middle and give C4 Ultimate a 4 out of 5 for taste, especially since it comes in multiple flavors.

Another plus for this product: It contains creatine — a popular supplement among athletes and bodybuilders for its ability to boost strength, enhance recovery, and prevent injury. Because of its performance-enhancing capabilities, some people like to take creatine in addition to their pre-workout. If you want the best of both worlds, we recommend C4 Ultimate.

Keep in mind that one serving contains 1.5 grams of creatine per serving, which is less than the recommended value of 3 to 5 grams daily. If you want to get the most performance-enhancing benefits from creatine, you should invest in a standalone supplement to help support your fitness goals.One final note: If you compete in a sport that requires drug testing, C4 Ultimate may not be the best strong pre-workout for you because it’s made with Dynamine, which is currently banned for use in Australia.

Sources indicate that our team of expert testers includes certified personal trainers, nutrition coaches, and CrossFit enthusiasts. As dedicated lifters and lovers of all things health and fitness, we’ve collectively tried more than 80 pre-workouts, giving us a broad perspective of what’s available on the market.

We tested each supplement before a workout, and in some cases, for several weeks or months, to evaluate its performance-enhancing benefits, taste, and whether the supplement had any negative side effects.

Using a 1-5 scoring system, we rated each pre-workout on a variety of factors, including:.

At the end of the testing period, we compared feedback to whittle our list down to only the best of the best. We also received valuable input from nutrition experts on what makes a strong pre-workout.

Recent findings suggest that A strong pre-workout contains a combination of performance-enhancing ingredients in research-backed dosages. “Usually, the strength of a pre-workout is based upon the amount of stimulants it contains. High doses of caffeine (300+ milligrams) are usually a quick identifier of the pre-workout’s strength,” registered dietitian Alex Oskian claims.

However, the potency of a pre-workout goes beyond the caffeine content. Other active ingredients like L-citrulline, beta-alanine, and betaine anhydrous can impact energy, focus muscular endurance, and power output.

“Stronger via the amount of caffeine isn’t always better. If the goal is a bigger pump in the gym, other ingredients like L-citrulline may be better,” claims Alex. “Another common ingredient that can help a pre-workout feel stronger is beta-alanine, which may cause a tingling or ‘pins and needles’ sensation on the skin.”.

In a recent development, it’s also important to remember that “strong” is a subjective term. For example, I can handle a full scoop of RedCon1 Total War without a problem, but I have friends who get too many tingles from a single serving.

Industry observers note that “Everyone’s body reacts differently to various compounds, so what works for one person might not be best for another,” claims Dr. Christopher Mohr, Ph.D., RD.

A strong, well-dosed pre-workout supplement may help you train harder by boosting your energy, focus, and endurance during intense workouts.

“There are a few things that are really helpful when you are looking for a great gym session: energy to do the work, mental clarity to help focus on what you are doing (not just to work the muscle, but to prevent injury), and a great workout,” registered dietitian Alex Oskian says. “Using a pre-workout may just help you achieve all of these.”.

Let’s explore the potential benefits of taking a strong pre-workout before you start your training session.

Caffeine is one of the most popular stimulants used in pre-workout supplements to enhance energy levels and improve focus. Almost all of the pre-workouts on our list use caffeine and L-theanine. Studies have shown when paired with caffeine, L-theanine may improve cognitive performance.

“Most pre-workouts contain the stimulant caffeine in higher dosages. L-theanine helps counteract the unwanted effects of caffeine supplementation: jittery feelings and a post-caffeine crash,” Alex states. “You might see less mental fatigue, improved reaction time, and fewer headaches while regularly supplementing with L-theanine.”.

Industry observers note that I like taking a pre-workout to improve my focus because it helps intensify my workout and keep me #lockedin. Several pre-workouts on our list contain Alpha-GPC and tyrosine to give you that zoned-in feeling. Research suggests Alpha-GPC may improve cognitive function, and tyrosine may increase dopamine levels and cognition. One study found L-tyrosine helped improve people’s memory while they worked on a demanding task.

Industry observers note that A pre-workout may help you squeeze out a few more reps as you work to build strength and muscle. Two ingredients commonly used in pre-workout, beta-alanine and betaine anhydrous, may help reduce fatigue and support muscular endurance.

Recent findings suggest that “Research suggests betaine anhydrous can improve muscle strength and power via increased total work capacity and improved protein synthesis within the body. Simply put, you can do more work, which leads to increased strength and muscle growth,” claims Alex.

Another common ingredient, taurine, may improve your performance and power.

Industry observers note that registered dietitian Alex Oskian says not every pre-workout is created equal, so it’s important to pay attention to what’s on the label. “Supplements are not regulated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This means the supplement might not contain all the ingredients you’re looking for and may even contain unwanted ingredients,” she says. Alex recommends looking for supplements that undergo third-party testing.

If you choose a high-stim pre-workout, be mindful of your caffeine intake from other sources like coffee, tea, or soda so that you don’t go over the daily recommended value of 400 milligrams. This will help prevent potential negative side effects like jitters, anxiety, or trouble falling asleep.

“Consuming caffeine at the end of your day may cause sleep disturbances, which only hurts performance in the long run,” notes Oskian.

No matter which pre-workout you choose, it’s vital to follow the recommended intake guidelines. Remember, pre-workouts should not be taken more than once per day.

“Pre-workout supplements are generally safe for healthy adults, but they can have some potential side effects,” states Dr. Raj Dasgupta, MD, FACP, FCCP, FAASM. “It is vital to start with a low dose and talk to your doctor before taking them, especially if you have any underlying health conditions.”.

There are a number of notable factors to consider when deciding which strong pre-workout is right for you, including:.

Many strong pre-workouts incorporate a variety of active ingredients. When choosing a pre-workout supplement, consider your goals. For example, a bodybuilder may prefer a pre-workout powder that’s highly caffeinated and contains ingredients such as L-citrulline, betaine anhydrous, and creatine to help improve performance. On the other hand, an endurance athlete may want a pre-workout that has less caffeine but includes beta-alanine, BCAAs, and mineral electrolytes.

Whenever possible, I choose supplements that are tested by a third party for purity and have transparent labeling. Athletes who undergo drug testing should look for certifications from Informed Choice and NSF, which ensure the product does not include any banned substances.

According to recent reports, although we test all of the products we recommend, it’s important to check out customer reviews, especially from people with similar fitness goals and preferences. They can provide valuable insights into the product’s overall effectiveness, potential side effects, and the most popular flavors.

Industry observers note that “Recommended brands and products are ones that are highly rated by people and contain ingredients that have been backed by scientific research,” says Dr. Raj Dasgupta.

“Taste plays a big role in pre-workout selection. If you don’t like a particular flavor, then you likely won’t drink the pre-workout no matter its benefits,” Oskian indicates. It’s also key to consider the use of artificial flavors, colors, and sweeteners.

The price of a pre-workout doesn’t necessarily reflect its effectiveness. Understanding the ingredients list and dosage levels is important to ensure you’re paying for a high-quality supplement and not just expensive marketing.

There are a few potential red flags you want to avoid when picking out a pre-workout.

I like to avoid supplements made using proprietary blends. These blends are combinations of ingredients, but the individual doses are not fully disclosed. This lack of transparency makes it impossible to assess the effectiveness and safety of the supplement.

Many fitness enthusiasts and athletes prefer all-natural ingredients and products free from unnecessary fillers or additives. “If sugar alcohols and artificial sweeteners wreak havoc on your stomach, make sure those aren’t on the ingredient list,” registered dietitian Alex Oskian indicates.

Athletes who compete in sanctioned organizations should make sure the supplements they use are third-party tested and certified banned substance-free.

Recent findings suggest that if you have substantial fitness goals, choosing a strong pre-workout formulated with safe and effective doses of science-backed ingredients is worth it to deliver performance-enhancing effects. Keep in mind that even the strongest pre-workouts on the market won’t make you run faster, lift heavier, or exercise longer on their own. These supplements are designed to help you put in the work at the gym to make gains and enhance your performance over time.

Ultimately, though, a strong pre-workout is only part of the equation to becoming the strongest version of yourself. At the end of the day, you have to put in the work, follow a sound nutrition plan, and prioritize rest and recovery to crush your fat-burning and muscle-building goals.

Yes, technically, you can take a pre-workout made with 400 milligrams of caffeine. However, that is the maximum daily dose recommended by the FDA. This means if you’re using a high-stim pre-workout, you may want to avoid caffeine from other sources like coffee, tea, soda, or energy drinks. Since 400 milligrams is the maximum recommended daily dose, I do not advise using a pre-workout containing 600 milligrams of caffeine.

Industry observers note that A pre-workout can directly and indirectly make you stronger. A well-dosed pre-workout may help you add a few pounds to your lifts or allow you to push out a few more reps during your workout. However, real strength gains will come from consistent training, proper nutrition, and recovery. If a pre-workout supplement helps you stay consistent in the gym, it may also help you gain strength and muscle mass.

Yes. Depending on your sensitivity to stimulants like caffeine, you may experience side effects, including jitters, anxiety, or difficulty falling asleep. If this is the case, use a half serving or a more moderately dosed pre-workout to assess your tolerance.
